nodes.name: Passive imaging problem (P): recover pipe geometry from a single-location measurement
nodes.statement: \tag{P} \parbox{\dimexpr\linewidth-2cm}{ \strut Suppose the fluid pressure or flow is measured at a single location in a pipe, with little to no information about the source signals, such as incident or source waves. Can the internal geometry of the pipe be recovered? \strut }
nodes.statement_short: Can a pipe's internal geometry be recovered from fluid pressure/flow measured at one location with unknown sources?
nodes.label: quote:ideal-problem

nodes.name: Admissible function A
nodes.statement: A function $A : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is called admissible if there are points $x_+> x_- > 0$ and a constant $A_\infty >0$ such that \begin{align} &A \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}), \\ & A > 0, \\ & A (x) = 1 , \quad \text{for every} \quad x < x_- , \\ &A (x) = A_\infty, , \quad \text{for every } \quad x > x_+. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: A smooth positive function equal to 1 left of $x_->0$ and to a constant $A_\infty>0$ right of $x_+$.
nodes.label: def:admissible

nodes.name: Admissibility conditions
nodes.statement: &A \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}), \\ & A > 0, \\ & A (x) = 1 , \quad \text{for every} \quad x < x_- , \\ &A (x) = A_\infty, , \quad \text{for every } \quad x > x_+.
nodes.label: thirdco

nodes.name: Normalisation of A at minus infinity
nodes.statement: The condition \eqref{thirdco} could be replaced with $A (x) = A_{-\infty}$, $\forall x < x_-$, where $A_{-\infty} >0 $ is a constant. One can always choose units such that $ A_{-\infty} = 1$, however.

nodes.name: Smooth cut-off chi
nodes.statement: Let $t \mapsto \chi(t)$ be a smooth cut-off function that equals $1$ for large $t$ and is supported in $(0,\infty)$. That is; $\chi \in C^\infty( \mathbb{R}) $, $\text{supp} (\chi) \subset (0,\infty)$ and $\chi-1 \in C^\infty_c(0,\infty)$.

nodes.name: White noise realisation omega
nodes.statement: Let $\omega \in \mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R})$ be an arbitrary element in the Gaussian white noise space $(\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}), \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$, see Section \ref{Gaussi} for more details.

nodes.name: White-noise driven wave u and operator square_A
nodes.statement: Considering $\chi \omega$ as the Neumann boundary value, the wave $u$ in $(0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}$ generated by the signal is modeled by \begin{align} &\square_A u (x,t) = 0 \quad \text{for} \quad (x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R} \\ &u(x,t) = 0 , \quad \text{for} \quad (x,t) \in (0,\infty)\times (-\infty,0) \\ &\partial_x u (x,t) \big|_{x = 0} = \chi(t)\omega(t) , \quad \text{for} \quad t \in \mathbb{R}, \end{align} where $\square_A f = \partial_t^2 f - \partial_x^2 f - (\partial_x A / A) \partial_x f$.
nodes.statement_short: The wave $u$ solves $\square_A u=0$ on the half-line, vanishes for $t<0$, with Neumann data $\chi\omega$ at $x=0$.

nodes.name: Space of smooth functions
nodes.statement: Let $C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ stand for the space of smooth functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

nodes.name: Compactly supported smooth functions
nodes.statement: We denote by $C^\infty_c(\mathbb{R}^n)$ the space of compactly supported elements in $C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

nodes.name: Smooth functions supported in K
nodes.statement: For a compact $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, let $C^\infty_K (\mathbb{R}^n)$ stand for functions $\phi \in C^\infty_c (\mathbb{R}^n)$ supported in $K$.

nodes.name: Seminorms on C_K^infty
nodes.statement: Each $C_{K}^\infty( \mathbb{R}^n)$ admits a Fr\'echet space topology induced by the seminorms \[ \| \phi \|_{k,K} := \sum_{|\alpha| \leq k} \sup_{x\in K} | \partial^\alpha \phi(x) |, \quad k =0,1,2,3\dots \]

nodes.name: C_c^infty as union of C_{K_j}^infty
nodes.statement: For any nested sequence $K_1 \subset K_2 \subset K_3 \subset \cdots$ of compact sets (e.g. $K_j = \bar{B}(0,j)$) such that $\bigcup_{j\in \mathbb{N}} K_j = \mathbb{R}^n$ we have $C_c^\infty ( \mathbb{R}^n) = \bigcup_{j \in \mathbb{N}} C_{K_j}^\infty$.

nodes.name: Inductive limit topology
nodes.statement: We equip the space $C_c^\infty ( \mathbb{R}^n ) $ with the inductive limit topology, that is, the largest topology for which the trivial inclusion maps $ C_K^\infty ( \mathbb{R}^n ) \hookrightarrow C_c^\infty ( \mathbb{R}^n ) $ are continuous.

nodes.name: Test functions
nodes.statement: The elements of $C_c^\infty ( \mathbb{R}^n ) $ are called smooth (compactly supported) test functions.

nodes.name: Distributions D'
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ be the dual space of $C^\infty_c (\mathbb{R}^n)$.

nodes.name: Seminorm characterisation of distributions
nodes.statement: It follows that a linear map $u : C^\infty_c ( \mathbb{R}^n) \to \mathbb{C} $ lies in $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ if and only if for every compact $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ there is a constant $C\geq 0$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ such that \begin{equation} | \langle u, \phi \rangle | \leq C \| \phi \|_{k,K} \end{equation} for every $\phi \in C_K^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$.
conclusions: lies in $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ if and only if for every compact $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ there is a constant $C\geq 0$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ such that \begin{equation}\label{distiey} | \langle u, \phi \rangle | \leq C \| \phi \|_{k,K} \end{equation} for every $\phi \in C_K^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$
equivalent_conditions: for every compact $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ there is a constant $C\geq 0$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$ such that \begin{equation}\label{distiey} | \langle u, \phi \rangle | \leq C \| \phi \|_{k,K} \end{equation} for every $\phi \in C_K^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$
nodes.statement_short: A linear functional on test functions is a distribution iff it is bounded by a $C^k$ seminorm on each compact.

nodes.name: Distribution seminorm bound
nodes.statement: | \langle u, \phi \rangle | \leq C \| \phi \|_{k,K}
nodes.label: distiey

nodes.name: Compactly supported distributions E'
nodes.statement: The space of compactly supported distributions in $\mathbb{R}^n$ shall be denoted by $\mathcal{E}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

nodes.name: Punctured space
nodes.statement: Denote $\dot{\mathbb{R}}^n := \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{0\}. $

nodes.name: Paley-Wiener theorem
nodes.statement: By Paley-Wiener theorem, a distribution $u \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is smooth in a neighbourhood of $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ if and only if there is $\phi \in C^\infty_c (\mathbb{R}^n)$ such that $\phi(x) \neq 0$ and \begin{equation} \widehat{\phi u} (\xi ) = O( |\xi|^{-N} ), \end{equation} for every $\xi \in \dot{\mathbb{R}}^n $ and $N \in \mathbb{N}$ as $|\xi| \to \infty$. Here $\widehat{\phi u}$ stands for the Fourier transform of $\phi u \in \mathcal{E}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$. That is; \[ \widehat{\phi u}( \xi) = \langle e^{-i(\cdot,\xi)} u , \phi \rangle . \]

nodes.name: Wave front set
nodes.statement: The wave front set $WF(u) \subset \mathbb{R}^{n} \times \dot{\mathbb{R}}^n $ of $u \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ can be defined as the complement of all $(x_0, \xi_0) \in \mathbb{R}^{n} \times \dot{\mathbb{R}}^n $ for which there exists an open neighbourhood $U $ of $x_0$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$, an open conic neighbourhood $V$ of $\xi_0$ in $\dot{\mathbb{R}}^n$ and a test function $\phi \in C_c^\infty(U)$, $\phi (x_0) \neq 0$ such that for every $N \in \mathbb{N}$ there is a constant $C\geq 0$ satisfying the estimate \[ | \widehat{\phi u} ( \xi ) | \leq C \langle \xi \rangle^{-N} . \] in $V$. Here $\langle \xi \rangle := ( 1 + |\xi|^2)^{1/2} $.
nodes.section: 2.2 The wave front set of a distribution
nodes.statement_short: $WF(u)$ is the complement of the points $(x_0,\xi_0)$ near which some localisation of $u$ has rapidly decaying Fourier transform in a cone around $\xi_0$.

nodes.name: Singular support
nodes.statement: The image of $WF(u)$ in the projection $(x,\theta) \mapsto x$ is called the singular support of $u$. It is denoted by $\text{singsupp}(u)$.
nodes.section: 2.2 The wave front set of a distribution

nodes.name: Wave front set of the Dirac delta
nodes.statement: Let $\delta_0 \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}^n) $ be the Dirac delta, defined by \[ \langle \delta_0 , \phi \rangle := \phi(0), \quad \phi \in C^\infty_c( \mathbb{R}^n) . \] The wave front set and singular support of $\delta_0$ are \[ WF ( \delta_0 ) = \{0\} \times \dot{\mathbb{R}}^n \quad \quad \text{and} \quad \quad \text{singsupp}(\delta_0) = \{0\}, \] respectively.
nodes.section: 2.2 The wave front set of a distribution

nodes.name: Wave front set of a half-space characteristic function
nodes.statement: Let $ u \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}^2) $, be the characteristic function of the half-space $\mathbb{R}_+ \times \mathbb{R}$. As a distribution, \[ \langle u , \phi \rangle = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{0}^\infty \phi(x,y) dxdy, \quad \phi \in C_c^\infty( \mathbb{R}^2) . \] The wave front set and singular support of $u$ are \[ WF(u) = \{0\} \times \mathbb{R} \times \dot{\mathbb{R}} \times \{0\} \] and \[ \text{singsupp}(u) = \{0\} \times \mathbb{R}, \] respectively.
nodes.section: 2.2 The wave front set of a distribution

nodes.name: Closed conic set Sigma
nodes.statement: Let $\Sigma $ be a closed conic set in the punctured cotangent bundle $(T^* \mathbb{R}^n) \setminus \{0\} = \mathbb{R}^n \times \dot{\mathbb{R}}^n$.

nodes.name: Space D'_Sigma
nodes.statement: Define \[ \mathcal{D}_{\Sigma}'(\mathbb{R}^n) := \{ u \in \mathcal{D}'( \mathbb{R}^n ) : WF(u) \subset \Sigma \} . \]

nodes.name: Seminorms rho_{N,Gamma,phi}
nodes.statement: Hence, we may consider the seminorms \begin{equation} \rho_{N,\Gamma,\phi}( u ) := \sup_{\xi \in \Gamma} | \xi |^N | \widehat{u \phi }( \xi ) | \end{equation} where $N \in \mathbb{N}$, $\phi \in C_c^\infty( \mathbb{R}^n) $ and $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{R}^n $ is a closed conic set such that $\text{supp} (\phi) \times \Gamma $ is disjoint of $\Sigma$.

nodes.name: Seminorm rho
nodes.statement: \rho_{N,\Gamma,\phi}( u ) := \sup_{\xi \in \Gamma} | \xi |^N | \widehat{u \phi }( \xi ) |
nodes.label: gaborseminorm

nodes.name: Topology of D'_Sigma
nodes.statement: We equip $\mathcal{D}_\Sigma'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ with the topology generated by this family of seminorms and the subspace topology inherited from $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

nodes.name: Convergence in D'_Sigma
nodes.statement: A sequence $u_j$, $j=1,2,3,\dots$ of elements in $\mathcal{D}_\Sigma'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ converges to an element $u$ in $\mathcal{D}_\Sigma'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ if and only if it converges to $u$ in $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ (i.e. $\langle u_j , \varphi \rangle \to \langle u , \varphi \rangle $ for every $\varphi \in C_c^\infty( \mathbb{R}^n) $) and $ \rho_{N,\Gamma,\phi}( u-u_j ) \to 0$ for all $N\in \mathbb{N}$, $\phi \in C_c^\infty( \mathbb{R}^n) $ and closed conic sets $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{R}^n $ with $\text{supp}(\phi) \times \Gamma $ disjoint of $\Sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: Convergence in $\mathcal{D}_\Sigma'$ means convergence in $\mathcal{D}'$ plus convergence in every seminorm $\rho_{N,\Gamma,\phi}$.

nodes.name: Schwartz space
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ be the Schwartz space of rapidly decreasing smooth functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

nodes.name: Tempered distributions
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ stand for the dual space of $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. The space $\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is known as the space of tempered distributions.

nodes.name: Cylindrical sigma-algebra
nodes.statement: We equip $\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ with the cylindrical $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{F}:=\text{Cyl} ( \mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^n))$.

nodes.name: Bochner-Minlos theorem
nodes.statement: The Bochner-Minlos theorem \cite[Theorem 2.1]{hida-lectures-book} implies the existence and uniqueness of Gaussian white noise probability measure $\mathbb{P}$ on $\mathcal{F}$.
conclusions: the existence and uniqueness of Gaussian white noise probability measure $\mathbb{P}$ on $\mathcal{F}$

nodes.name: Gaussian white noise measure
nodes.statement: This measure is typically defined via the property \[ \mathbb{E} ( e^{i \langle \cdot, \phi \rangle } ) = e^{- \frac{1}{2} \| \phi \|^2_{L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)} }, \quad \phi \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^n), \] where $\mathbb{E} ( e^{i \langle \cdot, \phi \rangle } ) $ stands for the characteristic function \[ \mathbb{E} ( e^{i \langle \cdot, \phi \rangle } ) = \int_{\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^n) } e^{i \langle \omega , \phi \rangle } \mu (d\omega). \]
nodes.statement_short: White noise measure: characteristic functional $\mathbb{E} e^{i\langle\cdot,\phi\rangle}=e^{-\|\phi\|^2_{L^2}/2}$.

nodes.name: White noise probability space
nodes.statement: The probability space $(\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^n), \mathcal{F} , \mathbb{P} )$ is called the white noise probability space.

nodes.name: W_phi
nodes.statement: Let us write $W_\phi := \langle \cdot, \phi \rangle $ for $\phi \in \mathcal{S}({\mathbb{R}^n})$.

nodes.name: White noise isometry
nodes.statement: It follows from the definition above that white noise admits the isometry \begin{equation} \mathbb{E} W_\phi^2 = \| \phi \|^2_{L^2} \end{equation} (cf. {It\^o} isometry).

nodes.name: White noise isometry (2.4)
nodes.statement: \mathbb{E} W_\phi^2 = \| \phi \|^2_{L^2}
nodes.label: itolike

nodes.name: White noise as derivative of Brownian motion
nodes.statement: It follows from \eqref{itolike} that $W_\phi $ can be defined as a $L^2 (\mathbb{P})$-function for every $\phi \in L^2 ( \mathbb{R}^d)$ by considering the limit $W_\phi := \lim_{n \to \infty} W_{ \phi_n} $ in $L^2(\mathbb{P})$, where $\phi_n$ stand for Schwartz functions converging to $\phi$ in $L^2 ( \mathbb{R}^d)$. This extension can be used to define Brownian motion: For simplicity, let us consider the 1-parameter case $d=1$. The multi-parameter construction is analogous. Let $ \chi_{[0,t)} $ for $t \geq 0$ be the characteristic function of the interval $[0,t)$. It is straightforward to check that the process $B_t := W_{\chi_{[0,t)} } $ is a single-parameter Brownian motion. White noise, as a stochastic process over $t \geq 0$, can therefore be thought as the distributional derivative $\partial_t B_t$. This is sometimes taken as a definition of white noise. Notice that the derivative $\partial_t B_t$ does not exist in the classical sense, in fact, Brownian motion is nowhere differentiable.
nodes.statement_short: Extending $W_\phi$ to $L^2$ gives Brownian motion $B_t=W_{\chi_{[0,t)}}$, and white noise is its distributional derivative.

nodes.name: Coefficient A in Section 3
nodes.statement: In this section, $A$ stands for a strictly positive smooth function $A : \mathbb{R} \to (0,\infty)$ with $\text{supp}(A-1) \subset (0,\infty)$.

nodes.name: Wave operator square_A
nodes.statement: Define the {(1+1)-}dimensional wave operator \[ \square_A : \mathcal{D}'( \mathbb{R}^2 ) \to \mathcal{D}'( \mathbb{R}^2 ) \] by \[ \square_A u(x,t) := \partial_t^2u (x,t) - \frac{1}{A(x)} \partial_x ( A(x) \partial_x u(x,t) ). \]

nodes.name: Principal symbol p
nodes.statement: The principal symbol (see e.g. \cite{grigis-sjostrand}) of $\square_A$ is represented (away from the origin) by the function \[ p(x,t,\xi_x,\xi_t) = - \xi_t^2 + \xi_x^2 \] on $ (x,t,\xi_x,\xi_t) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \times \dot{\mathbb{R}}^2$.

nodes.name: Characteristic variety Sigma
nodes.statement: The associated characteristic variety is the null covector bundle \[ \Sigma := \ker p \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \times \dot{\mathbb{R}}^2. \]

nodes.name: Initial-boundary value problem (3.1)-(3.3)
nodes.statement: Let $f \in \mathcal{D}' ( \mathbb{R} )$ such that $\text{supp} (f) \subset (t_0,\infty)$. Fix $\mu$ to be either $0$ or $1$. We consider the following initial-boundary value problem: \begin{align} &\square_A u (x,t)= 0 \quad \text{for} \quad (x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R} , \\ &u(x,t) = 0 , \quad \text{for} \quad (x,t) \in (0,\infty)\times (-\infty,t_0), \\ &\partial_x^\mu u (x,t) \big|_{x = 0} = f(t), \quad \text{for} \quad t \in \mathbb{R}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Wave equation $\square_A u=0$ on $x>0$, zero before $t_0$, with Dirichlet ($\mu=0$) or Neumann ($\mu=1$) boundary data $f$.

nodes.name: Pull-back to the boundary on D'_Sigma
nodes.statement: Indeed, the inclusion \begin{align} \iota_{x=0} : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2, \quad \iota_{x=0} (t) := (0,t) \in \mathbb{R}^2, \end{align} generates (see \cite[Theorem 2.5.11']{hormanderFIO1}) a sequentially continuous pull-back \begin{align} \iota^*_{x=0} : \mathcal{D}_{\Sigma}'(\mathbb{R}^2) \to \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}) \end{align} which can be applied to extend the standard boundary trace operator $u \mapsto u |_{x=0}$ as well as the Neumann data $u \mapsto \partial_x u |_{x=0}$.
nodes.statement_short: The boundary inclusion induces a sequentially continuous pull-back $\mathcal{D}'_\Sigma(\mathbb{R}^2)\to\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})$, extending traces.

nodes.statement: Define $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})_{t_0} := \{ u \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}) : \operatorname{supp} (u) \subset (t_0, \infty) \} \subset \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}) $ and equip it with the subspace topology inherited from $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})$.

nodes.name: Existence of solutions
nodes.statement: Let $f \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})_{t_0}$ and choose $\mu$ to be either $0$ or $1$. Then there exists $u \in \mathcal{D}_{\Sigma}'(\mathbb{R}^2) $ that satisfies \eqref{ibvp1}-\eqref{ibvp4} and depends continuously on $f$ in $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})_{t_0}$.
conclusions: there exists $u \in \mathcal{D}_{\Sigma}'(\mathbb{R}^2) $ that satisfies \eqref{ibvp1}-\eqref{ibvp4} and depends continuously on $f$ in $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})_{t_0}$.

nodes.name: Local existence of IBVP solutions via Cauchy problem
nodes.statement: Let $f \in \mathcal{E}' (\mathbb{R})$ be supported in $(0,\infty)$ and let $\mu$ be either $0$ or $1$. Fix small $s,\delta>0$ such that $\text{supp} (f) \subset (s,\infty) $ and $A|_{(-\infty , \delta)} = 1$. Then there is a solution $u = u_{f} \in \mathcal{D}_{\Sigma}'(\mathbb{R}^2) $ to \begin{align} &\square_A u = 0 \quad \text{in} \quad (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}, \\ &u = 0 , \quad \text{in} \quad (0,\infty) \times (-\infty,0), \\ &\partial_x^\mu u \big|_{x = 0} = f, \quad \text{in} \quad (-\infty, \ 2\delta + s) . \end{align} that vanishes in the wedge $W := \{ (x,t) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : |t| <x +s\}$ and depends continuously on $f$ with respect to the topology (see Section \ref{subsection_test-functions}) of $\mathcal{E}'(\mathbb{R})$. { Moreover, the solution $u=u_f$ does not depend of the choice of $s \in (0, \min \operatorname{supp} (f))$ and is linear as a function of elements $f \in \mathcal{E}'(\mathbb{R})$ supported in $(0,\infty)$. }
conclusions: there is a solution $u = u_{f} \in \mathcal{D}_{\Sigma}'(\mathbb{R}^2) $ to
the solution $u=u_f$ does not depend of the choice of $s \in (0, \min \operatorname{supp} (f))$ and is linear as a function of elements $f \in \mathcal{E}'(\mathbb{R})$ supported in $(0,\infty)$.
nodes.statement_short: For compactly supported $f$, a solution of the IBVP with data $f$ up to time $2\delta+s$ exists, vanishes in a wedge, and is linear and continuous in $f$.

nodes.statement: We may assume that $t_0 = 0$. Let { $\tau_T \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ stand for a cut-off that equals $1$ near $[-T, T]$, $T>0$ and define $f_0^T := f$. Since $u_j^{{T}}$ vanishes in the wedge \[ W_{s_j} := \{ (x,t) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : |t| <x +s_j\} \] and $\lim_{j \to \infty} s_j = \infty$, the sum $u^{{T}} := \sum_{j \geq 0} u_j^{{T}}$ is well defined in $\mathcal{D}'_\Sigma(\mathbb{R}^2)$. Indeed, only finite number of terms $u_j^{{T}}$ are non-zero in a relatively compact neighbourhood. Moreover, each $u_j^{{T}}$ depends continuously on $\tau_T f$ {which further depends continuously on $f$. } Hence, $u^{T}$ is continuous as a function of $f \in {\mathcal{D}}_{0}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$. T { Let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^2 $ be compact. Let us show that $u^T = u^{T_K}$ near $K$ for $T \geq T_K := 2\min \{ r \geq 0 : K \subset W_r \}$, where $W_r $ stands for the wedge \[ W_r := \{ (x,t) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : |t| < x+r\}. \] This implies that the weak limit $\lim_{T \to \infty} u^T$ exists and remains continuous in $f$. Define $v:= u^T-u^{T_K}$, $T \geq T_K$. Let $N$ be so large that $T_K < s_N $ and therefore $W_{T_K} \subset W_{s_N}$. Then $u_j^T $ vanishes near $W_{T_K}$ for every $j > N$ and hence $u^T = \sum_{0\leq j \leq N} u_j^T$ near $W_{T_K} $. Moreover, \[ \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x=0} = \sum_{0\leq j \leq N} \partial_x^\mu u_j^T|_{x=0} \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty,T_K]. \] We have \begin{align} f_N^T &= f_{N-1}^T - \partial_x^\mu u_{N-1}^T|_{x=0} \\ &= f_{N-2}^T - \partial_x^\mu u_{N-2}^T|_{x=0} - \partial_x^\mu u_{N-1}^T |_{x=0} \\ \vdots \\ &= f_0^T - \sum_{0 \leq j\leq N-1} \partial_x^\mu u_{j}^T |_{x=0} \\ &= f - \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x=0} + \partial_x^\mu u_N^T|_{x=0} \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty,T_K] \\ &= f - \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x=0} + \tau_T f_N^T \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty,T_K]. \end{align} Hence, \[ \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x=0} = f - (1-\tau_T) f_N^T \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty, T_K]. \] Since $T \geq T_K$, the cut-off $(1-\tau_T)$ in the latter term vanishes near $(-\infty, T_K]$ and we arrive at \begin{equation} \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x=0} = f \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty, T_K]. \end{equation} By the same argument, \[ \partial_x^\mu u^{T_K} |_{x=0} = f- (1-\tau_{T_K}) f_N^{T_K} = f \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty, T_{K}]. \] Thus, \[ \partial_x^\mu v|_{x=0} = (\tau_T- \tau_{T_K}) f \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty, T_K]. \] As the cut-off $(\tau_T- \tau_{T_K})$ on the right hand side is supported in $(T_K , \infty)$, we obtain \[ \text{supp} (\partial_{x}^\mu v |_{x=0}) \subset (T_K , \infty). \] By the linearity statement in Lemma \ref{weaker-exist}, $v$ is a wave with boundary value as above. Moreover, $v$ vanishes in the wedge \[ \{ (x,t) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : |t| <x +T_K\} . \] In particular, it vanishes near $K$. Thus, \[ u^T = u^{T_K} - v = u^{T_K} \quad \text{near} \quad K. \] As shown above, the weak limit $u:= \lim_{T \to \infty} u^T $ exists and is continuous in $f$. Moreover, it equals $u^{T_K}$ near compact $K \subset (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}$. In particular, \[ \langle u , \varphi \rangle = \langle u^{T} , \varphi \rangle = \langle u^{T_K} , \varphi \rangle , \] for $\varphi \in C_c^\infty((0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R})$ and $T \geq T_K$, where $K$ is such that $\operatorname{supp}(\varphi) \subset K$. Since $\square_A$ is a local operator and $ \square_A u^{T_K} = 0$, we have \[ \langle \square_A u , \varphi \rangle = \langle u , \square_A \varphi \rangle = \langle u^{T_K} , \square_A \varphi \rangle = \langle \square_A u^{T_K} , \varphi \rangle = 0. \] That is, $\square_A u =0$. Finally, let us show that $\partial_x^\mu u|_{x=0} = f$. Fix arbitrary $\phi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ and set $K := [-1,1] \times \operatorname{supp}(\phi) $. With this choice, $\partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x= 0} = f$ holds near $(-\infty, T_K] $ for $T \geq T_K$ by \eqref{qoo}. In particular, it holds near the support of $\phi$. By continuity of $\partial_x^\mu$ and the boundary restriction, \[ \langle \partial_x^\mu u |_{x= 0} , \phi \rangle = \langle \partial_x^\mu (\lim_{T \to \infty} u^T ) |_{x= 0} , \phi \rangle = \lim_{T \to \infty} \langle \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x= 0} , \phi \rangle = \lim_{T \to \infty}\langle f, \phi \rangle = \langle f, \phi \rangle. \] This finishes the proof. }
nodes.statement_short: Iterate Lemma 3.2 to correct the boundary defect, sum the wedge-vanishing corrections, then pass to the limit $T\to\infty$ of time cut-offs.

nodes.name: WLOG t_0 = 0
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $t_0=0$
nodes.statement: We may assume that $t_0 = 0$.

nodes.name: First cut-off solution
nodes.statement_short: Take the Lemma 3.2 solution for the cut-off data $\tau_T f$
nodes.statement: Let { $\tau_T \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ stand for a cut-off that equals $1$ near $[-T, T]$, $T>0$ and define $f_0^T := f$. Let $ u_{0}^T$ be the solution in Lemma \ref{weaker-exist} with $\tau_T f_0^T$ as the boundary value. } Then $\partial_x^\mu u_0^{{T}} |_{x = 0} = {\tau_T} f $ in $ (-\infty, 2\delta + s) $.

nodes.name: Iterative boundary corrections
nodes.statement_short: Recursively correct the boundary defect with Lemma 3.2 solutions on later wedges
nodes.statement: Set $ f_j^T := f_{j-1}^T- \partial_x^\mu u_{j-1}^T |_{x=0} $ and define $u_{j}^{{T}}$, $j=1,2,3,\dots$ recursively as the solution in Lemma \ref{weaker-exist} but with the function ${\tau_T} f_j^T$ substituted for $f$ and $s_j := s_{j-1} + \delta = s + j \delta$ substituted for $s$.

nodes.name: Sum of corrections well defined
nodes.statement_short: The corrections vanish in growing wedges, so their sum $u^T$ is well defined and continuous in $f$
nodes.statement: Since $u_j^{{T}}$ vanishes in the wedge \[ W_{s_j} := \{ (x,t) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : |t| <x +s_j\} \] and $\lim_{j \to \infty} s_j = \infty$, the sum $u^{{T}} := \sum_{j \geq 0} u_j^{{T}}$ is well defined in $\mathcal{D}'_\Sigma(\mathbb{R}^2)$. Indeed, only finite number of terms $u_j^{{T}}$ are non-zero in a relatively compact neighbourhood. Moreover, each $u_j^{{T}}$ depends continuously on $\tau_T f$ {which further depends continuously on $f$. } Hence, $u^{T}$ is continuous as a function of $f \in {\mathcal{D}}_{0}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

nodes.name: Claim: u^T stabilises near compacts
nodes.statement_short: Show $u^T=u^{T_K}$ near a compact $K$ for $T\ge T_K$
nodes.statement: Let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^2 $ be compact. Let us show that $u^T = u^{T_K}$ near $K$ for $T \geq T_K := 2\min \{ r \geq 0 : K \subset W_r \}$, where $W_r $ stands for the wedge \[ W_r := \{ (x,t) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : |t| < x+r\}. \] This implies that the weak limit $\lim_{T \to \infty} u^T$ exists and remains continuous in $f$. Define $v:= u^T-u^{T_K}$, $T \geq T_K$. Let $N$ be so large that $T_K < s_N $ and therefore $W_{T_K} \subset W_{s_N}$. Then $u_j^T $ vanishes near $W_{T_K}$ for every $j > N$ and hence $u^T = \sum_{0\leq j \leq N} u_j^T$ near $W_{T_K} $. Moreover, \[ \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x=0} = \sum_{0\leq j \leq N} \partial_x^\mu u_j^T|_{x=0} \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty,T_K]. \] We have \begin{align} f_N^T &= f_{N-1}^T - \partial_x^\mu u_{N-1}^T|_{x=0} \\ &= f_{N-2}^T - \partial_x^\mu u_{N-2}^T|_{x=0} - \partial_x^\mu u_{N-1}^T |_{x=0} \\ \vdots \\ &= f_0^T - \sum_{0 \leq j\leq N-1} \partial_x^\mu u_{j}^T |_{x=0} \\ &= f - \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x=0} + \partial_x^\mu u_N^T|_{x=0} \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty,T_K] \\ &= f - \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x=0} + \tau_T f_N^T \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty,T_K]. \end{align} Hence, \[ \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x=0} = f - (1-\tau_T) f_N^T \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty, T_K]. \] Since $T \geq T_K$, the cut-off $(1-\tau_T)$ in the latter term vanishes near $(-\infty, T_K]$ and we arrive at \begin{equation} \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x=0} = f \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty, T_K]. \end{equation} By the same argument, \[ \partial_x^\mu u^{T_K} |_{x=0} = f- (1-\tau_{T_K}) f_N^{T_K} = f \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty, T_{K}]. \] Thus, \[ \partial_x^\mu v|_{x=0} = (\tau_T- \tau_{T_K}) f \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty, T_K]. \] As the cut-off $(\tau_T- \tau_{T_K})$ on the right hand side is supported in $(T_K , \infty)$, we obtain \[ \text{supp} (\partial_{x}^\mu v |_{x=0}) \subset (T_K , \infty). \] By the linearity statement in Lemma \ref{weaker-exist}, $v$ is a wave with boundary value as above. Moreover, $v$ vanishes in the wedge \[ \{ (x,t) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : |t| <x +T_K\} . \] In particular, it vanishes near $K$. Thus, \[ u^T = u^{T_K} - v = u^{T_K} \quad \text{near} \quad K. \]

nodes.name: Purpose of the claim
nodes.statement_short: The claim yields the weak limit as $T\to\infty$
nodes.statement: Let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^2 $ be compact. Let us show that $u^T = u^{T_K}$ near $K$ for $T \geq T_K := 2\min \{ r \geq 0 : K \subset W_r \}$, where $W_r $ stands for the wedge \[ W_r := \{ (x,t) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : |t| < x+r\}. \] This implies that the weak limit $\lim_{T \to \infty} u^T$ exists and remains continuous in $f$.

nodes.name: Difference v and index N
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $v=u^T-u^{T_K}$ and $N$ with $T_K<s_N$
nodes.statement: Define $v:= u^T-u^{T_K}$, $T \geq T_K$. Let $N$ be so large that $T_K < s_N $ and therefore $W_{T_K} \subset W_{s_N}$.

nodes.name: Finite sum near the wedge
nodes.statement_short: Only finitely many corrections contribute near $W_{T_K}$
nodes.statement: Then $u_j^T $ vanishes near $W_{T_K}$ for every $j > N$ and hence $u^T = \sum_{0\leq j \leq N} u_j^T$ near $W_{T_K} $. Moreover, \[ \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x=0} = \sum_{0\leq j \leq N} \partial_x^\mu u_j^T|_{x=0} \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty,T_K]. \]

nodes.name: Telescoping boundary data
nodes.statement_short: Telescoping the corrections gives $\partial_x^\mu u^T|_{x=0}=f$ near $(-\infty,T_K]$
nodes.statement: We have \begin{align} f_N^T &= f_{N-1}^T - \partial_x^\mu u_{N-1}^T|_{x=0} \\ &= f_{N-2}^T - \partial_x^\mu u_{N-2}^T|_{x=0} - \partial_x^\mu u_{N-1}^T |_{x=0} \\ \vdots \\ &= f_0^T - \sum_{0 \leq j\leq N-1} \partial_x^\mu u_{j}^T |_{x=0} \\ &= f - \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x=0} + \partial_x^\mu u_N^T|_{x=0} \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty,T_K] \\ &= f - \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x=0} + \tau_T f_N^T \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty,T_K]. \end{align} Hence, \[ \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x=0} = f - (1-\tau_T) f_N^T \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty, T_K]. \] Since $T \geq T_K$, the cut-off $(1-\tau_T)$ in the latter term vanishes near $(-\infty, T_K]$ and we arrive at \begin{equation} \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x=0} = f \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty, T_K]. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Equation (3.9)
nodes.statement: f_N^T &= f_{N-1}^T - \partial_x^\mu u_{N-1}^T|_{x=0} \\ &= f_{N-2}^T - \partial_x^\mu u_{N-2}^T|_{x=0} - \partial_x^\mu u_{N-1}^T |_{x=0}

nodes.name: Equation (3.11)
nodes.statement: \vdots \\ &= f_0^T - \sum_{0 \leq j\leq N-1} \partial_x^\mu u_{j}^T |_{x=0} \\ &= f - \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x=0} + \partial_x^\mu u_N^T|_{x=0} \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty,T_K] \\ &= f - \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x=0} + \tau_T f_N^T \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty,T_K].

nodes.name: Recovered boundary data (3.15)
nodes.statement: \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x=0} = f \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty, T_K].
nodes.label: qoo

nodes.name: Boundary data of v
nodes.statement_short: The boundary data of $v$ is supported in $(T_K,\infty)$
nodes.statement: By the same argument, \[ \partial_x^\mu u^{T_K} |_{x=0} = f- (1-\tau_{T_K}) f_N^{T_K} = f \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty, T_{K}]. \] Thus, \[ \partial_x^\mu v|_{x=0} = (\tau_T- \tau_{T_K}) f \quad \text{near} \quad (-\infty, T_K]. \] As the cut-off $(\tau_T- \tau_{T_K})$ on the right hand side is supported in $(T_K , \infty)$, we obtain \[ \text{supp} (\partial_{x}^\mu v |_{x=0}) \subset (T_K , \infty). \]

nodes.name: v vanishes near K
nodes.statement_short: By linearity and finite speed, $v$ vanishes near $K$
nodes.statement: By the linearity statement in Lemma \ref{weaker-exist}, $v$ is a wave with boundary value as above. Moreover, $v$ vanishes in the wedge \[ \{ (x,t) \in \mathbb{R}^2 : |t| <x +T_K\} . \] In particular, it vanishes near $K$. Thus, \[ u^T = u^{T_K} - v = u^{T_K} \quad \text{near} \quad K. \]

nodes.name: Limit solves the wave equation
nodes.statement_short: The weak limit $u$ satisfies $\square_A u=0$ by locality
nodes.statement: As shown above, the weak limit $u:= \lim_{T \to \infty} u^T $ exists and is continuous in $f$. Moreover, it equals $u^{T_K}$ near compact $K \subset (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}$. In particular, \[ \langle u , \varphi \rangle = \langle u^{T} , \varphi \rangle = \langle u^{T_K} , \varphi \rangle , \] for $\varphi \in C_c^\infty((0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R})$ and $T \geq T_K$, where $K$ is such that $\operatorname{supp}(\varphi) \subset K$. Since $\square_A$ is a local operator and $ \square_A u^{T_K} = 0$, we have \[ \langle \square_A u , \varphi \rangle = \langle u , \square_A \varphi \rangle = \langle u^{T_K} , \square_A \varphi \rangle = \langle \square_A u^{T_K} , \varphi \rangle = 0. \] That is, $\square_A u =0$.

nodes.name: Limit has the boundary data
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of the trace gives $\partial_x^\mu u|_{x=0}=f$
nodes.statement: Finally, let us show that $\partial_x^\mu u|_{x=0} = f$. Fix arbitrary $\phi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ and set $K := [-1,1] \times \operatorname{supp}(\phi) $. With this choice, $\partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x= 0} = f$ holds near $(-\infty, T_K] $ for $T \geq T_K$ by \eqref{qoo}. In particular, it holds near the support of $\phi$. By continuity of $\partial_x^\mu$ and the boundary restriction, \[ \langle \partial_x^\mu u |_{x= 0} , \phi \rangle = \langle \partial_x^\mu (\lim_{T \to \infty} u^T ) |_{x= 0} , \phi \rangle = \lim_{T \to \infty} \langle \partial_x^\mu u^T |_{x= 0} , \phi \rangle = \lim_{T \to \infty}\langle f, \phi \rangle = \langle f, \phi \rangle. \] This finishes the proof.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement_short: Solve a Cauchy problem with reflected data, use d'Alembert's form near $x=0$ and finite speed of propagation, then cut off the past.

nodes.name: Cauchy problem well-posedness
nodes.statement_short: Recall well-posedness of the Cauchy problem (Duistermaat Th. 5.1.6)
nodes.statement: Let $f_0,f_1 \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})$. By \cite[Th. 5.1.6.]{duistermaat-FIOs}, there is a unique solution $u \in \mathcal{D}_\Sigma' (\mathbb{R}^2)$ to the Cauchy problem \begin{align} &\square_A u = 0 \quad \text{on} \quad \mathbb{R}^2, \\ & u|_{t=0} = f_0 \\ &\partial_t u |_{t=0} = f_1. \end{align} Moreover, the solution depends continuously on the data $(f_0,f_1)$. Indeed, the additional condition \cite[(5.1.10)]{duistermaat-FIOs} in the theorem is met.

nodes.name: Cauchy problem
nodes.statement: &\square_A u = 0 \quad \text{on} \quad \mathbb{R}^2, \\ & u|_{t=0} = f_0 \\ &\partial_t u |_{t=0} = f_1.

nodes.name: Idea: Cauchy problem gives the IBVP
nodes.statement_short: Plan: choose Cauchy data so the Cauchy solution solves the IBVP, then cut off the past
nodes.statement: Below we apply this with specific choice of $f_0$, $f_1$. The idea is that, with the right choice of Cauchy data, the solution of the Cauchy problem solves the initial-boundary value problem \eqref{ibvp11}-\eqref{ibvp44} away from $(0,\infty)\times (-\infty,-s]$. By cutting off the component of $\operatorname{supp} (u)$ in $(0,\infty)\times (-\infty,-s]$ we obtain a solution in the half-space $(0,\infty)\times \mathbb{R}$. Hence, the Cauchy problem in $\mathbb{R}^2$ can be used to construct solution to the initial-boundary value problem \eqref{ibvp11}-\eqref{ibvp44} in the half-space.}

nodes.name: Mollified Cauchy problem
nodes.statement_short: Define $u_\varepsilon$ by a Cauchy problem with mollified reflected data
nodes.statement: Let $\phi \in C^\infty_c( \mathbb{R}) $ be a mollifier and denote $\phi_\varepsilon = \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \phi \left( \frac{x}{\varepsilon} \right)$. Let $u_\epsilon \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^2)$ be the {global} solution to the following Cauchy problem: \begin{align} &\square_A u_\varepsilon = 0 \quad \text{on} \quad \mathbb{R}^2, \\ & u_\varepsilon |_{t=0} = (-1)^\mu \phi_\varepsilon * \tau^* f^{(-\mu)} , \\ &\partial_t u_\varepsilon |_{t=0} = (-1)^\mu \phi_\varepsilon * \tau^* f^{(1-\mu)} . \end{align} where $\tau : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $\tau (x) := -x$, $f^{(0)} (x) := f(x) $, $f^{(1)} (x):= \partial_x f(x) $ and $f^{(-1)}$ is the forward propagating inverse derivative, defined by \begin{align} \langle f^{(-1)}, \phi \rangle := -\langle f, \tilde\phi \rangle, \quad \tilde\phi(x) := \int_{-\infty}^{x } \phi(r) dr , \end{align} for every $\phi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$. Notice that this is well defined since $f$ is compactly supported. Moreover, $f^{(-\mu)} $ is supported in $(s,\infty)$.

nodes.name: Mollified Cauchy problem
nodes.statement: &\square_A u_\varepsilon = 0 \quad \text{on} \quad \mathbb{R}^2, \\ & u_\varepsilon |_{t=0} = (-1)^\mu \phi_\varepsilon * \tau^* f^{(-\mu)} , \\ &\partial_t u_\varepsilon |_{t=0} = (-1)^\mu \phi_\varepsilon * \tau^* f^{(1-\mu)} .
nodes.label: cauchy1

nodes.name: Forward inverse derivative
nodes.statement: \langle f^{(-1)}, \phi \rangle := -\langle f, \tilde\phi \rangle, \quad \tilde\phi(x) := \int_{-\infty}^{x } \phi(r) dr ,

nodes.name: Limit solution u_0
nodes.statement_short: The Cauchy solution $u_0$ is the limit of $u_\varepsilon$
nodes.statement: The solution $u_0$ associated with the data $(f_0,f_1) = ((-1)^\mu\tau^*f^{(-\mu)}, (-1)^\mu \tau^*f^{(1-\mu)})$ coincides with the limit $ \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} u_\varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Heuristic explanation
nodes.statement_short: Heuristic: for $A=1$ integrate along null lines; echoes from $x>\delta$ return only after a delay
nodes.statement: Let us shortly explain why we choose this wave. First, suppose we have a trivial profile $A=1$. Then the explicit expression for the wave $u_\varepsilon$ can be derived by integrating along the null lines $\{ x = c\pm t\}$ (cf. the local version of this argument below). In that case, we would find, after applying a cut-off, that $u_\varepsilon$ solves $\square_A u = 0$, $\partial^\mu_x u |_{x=0} = \phi_\varepsilon * f$ and $u = 0 = \partial_t u$ for $t<0$ for small $\varepsilon>0$. Taking the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$ would therefore give the solution to \eqref{ibvp11}-\eqref{ibvp44} (even for $\delta= \infty $) by continuity. The mollification in the data was introduced so that the integration along null curves would be meaningful. Somewhat similar argument could be made directly without the mollification. Notice that the Cauchy problem itself does not require smoothness. Let us now return to the case where $A$ is non-trivial in $(\delta, \infty)$. Although $A=1$ holds near the t-axis $\{x = 0\}$, the preceding argument is not valid anymore. The issue is the possibility of echoes originating from the region $x>\delta$. Nevertheless, such echoes reach the point $x=0$ only after a delay: the initial wave must first propagate into the region, and any scattered signal must then return to $x=0$. Consequently, the boundary value $\partial^\mu_x u |_{x=0} = \phi_\varepsilon * f$ is preserved for early times $t>0$. More precisely, this holds for $t \in (-\infty,2\delta +s)$ provided that $\varepsilon>0$ is sufficiently small.

nodes.name: General solution of the flat wave equation
nodes.statement_short: Near $x=0$ the operator is $\frac14\partial_0\partial_1$, so solutions are $F(z_0)+G(z_1)$
nodes.statement: Let us now do this in detail. As implied above,} the operator $\square_A$ reduces to the trivial wave operator ${ \square_1 =} \square = \partial_t^2 - \partial_x^2$ in the half space $ (-\infty,\delta ] \times \mathbb{R} $ for any sufficiently small $\delta >0$. It is easy to check that $ \square $ equals $\frac{1}{4} \partial_{0} \partial_{1}$ in the coordinates $(z_0,z_1) := (t-x, t+x)$. Integrating twice, one deduces that the general smooth solution to $\frac{1}{4} \partial_{0} \partial_{1} v = 0$ is \[ v(z_0,z_1) = F(z_0 ) + G(z_1) = (F \otimes 1) (z_0,z_1 ) + (1 \otimes G) (z_0,z_1) , \] where $F,G \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$. Moreover, if $ v_\varepsilon = F_\varepsilon \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes G_\varepsilon$ for $\varepsilon >0$ is a family of such solutions and the limit $\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} v_\varepsilon$ exists in $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}^2)$, we may choose $F_\varepsilon $ and $G_\varepsilon $ such that they converge individually to some distributions $ F_0 $ and $G_0 $.

nodes.name: d'Alembert form of u_epsilon
nodes.statement_short: Hence $u_\varepsilon=F_\varepsilon(t-x)+G_\varepsilon(t+x)$ near the boundary
nodes.statement: Hence, { the global solution $u_\varepsilon \in C^\infty ( \mathbb{R}^2)$ must be of the form} \begin{equation} u_\varepsilon (x,t) = F_\varepsilon (t-x ) + G_\varepsilon (t+x) \end{equation} in $ (-\infty,\delta] \times \mathbb{R} $ for some $F_\varepsilon,G_\varepsilon $ that converge in $ \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. {Notice that this expression holds even though the functions $F_\varepsilon,G_\varepsilon$ cannot be solved from local information alone.} Formally, we have \begin{equation} u_0 (x,t) = F_0 (t-x ) + G_0 (t+x) \end{equation} for $(x,t) \in (-\infty,\delta) \times \mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: d'Alembert form (3.23)
nodes.statement: u_\varepsilon (x,t) = F_\varepsilon (t-x ) + G_\varepsilon (t+x)
nodes.label: wqi

nodes.name: Rigorous d'Alembert form
nodes.statement_short: Make the d'Alembert form rigorous via pull-backs $\rho_\pm^*$
nodes.statement: For the rigorous expression, define $\rho_\pm : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R} $, $\rho_\pm (x,t) := t\pm x$ and extend the pull-backs $\rho^*_\pm$ into continuous operators $\rho_\pm^* : \mathcal{D}'( \mathbb{R} ) \to \mathcal{D}'( \mathbb{R}^2 )$ by applying the last identity in \[ \langle \rho^*v , \phi \rangle = \int_{\mathbb{R}^2} v(t\pm x) \phi(x,t) dt dx = \int_{\mathbb{R}^2} v(s ) \phi(x,s \mp x ) ds dx . \] That is, $\rho_\pm^*v = (\sigma_\pm )_* ( 1 \otimes v )$ where $\sigma_\pm : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is the diffeomorphism $\sigma_\pm (x,s) = (x,s \mp x)$. The identity \eqref{wqi} then reads \[ u_\varepsilon = \rho_-^* F_\varepsilon + \rho_+^* G_\varepsilon , \quad \text{in } \quad (-\infty,\delta] \times \mathbb{R} \] and taking the limit yields \begin{equation} u_0 = \rho_-^* F_0 + \rho_+^* G_0, \quad \text{in } \quad (-\infty,\delta) \times \mathbb{R} \end{equation} by the continuity of $ \rho_\pm^* $. This is the formal identity \eqref{wqi1} in a rigorous form.

nodes.name: Rigorous d'Alembert form (3.25)
nodes.statement: u_0 = \rho_-^* F_0 + \rho_+^* G_0, \quad \text{in } \quad (-\infty,\delta) \times \mathbb{R}
nodes.label: s11

nodes.name: Microlocal splitting
nodes.statement_short: Split $u_0$ into right- and left-moving components
nodes.statement: The two terms, $ \rho_-^* F_0 \in \mathcal{D}_{\Sigma^\rightarrow}' ( (-\infty,\delta) \times \mathbb{R} )$ and $ \rho_+^* G_0 \in \mathcal{D}_{\Sigma^\leftarrow}' ( (-\infty,\delta) \times \mathbb{R} )$, represent the components of $u_0$ propagating in the {respective} characteristic component \[ \Sigma^{\rightarrow} := \{ (x,t, - \lambda , \lambda) : \lambda \in \dot{\mathbb{R}}\}, \quad \Sigma^{\leftarrow} := \{ (x,t, \lambda , \lambda) : \lambda \in \dot{\mathbb{R}}\} \] towards the infinities $( \pm \infty , \infty)$ (i.e. to the right or left). In fact, we may split \[ u_0 = u_0^\rightarrow + u_0^\leftarrow, \quad u_0^{\rightarrow} \in \mathcal{D}_{\Sigma^{\rightarrow }}' ( \mathbb{R}^2 ), \quad u_0^{\leftarrow} \in \mathcal{D}_{\Sigma^{\leftarrow }}' ( \mathbb{R}^2 ) \] in the whole $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that $u_0^\rightarrow = \rho_-^* F_0$ and $u_0^\leftarrow = \rho_+^* G_0$ in $(-\infty , \delta) \times \mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Components vanish in W
nodes.statement_short: Finite speed of propagation makes both components constant, hence zero, in the wedge $W$
nodes.statement: Let $s>0 $ be such that $ \text{supp} (f) \subset (s ,\infty), $ as in the assumptions. Then the Cauchy data of $u_0$ is supported in $(-\infty ,-s)$ and $u_0$ vanishes in the wedge $W:= \{ (x,t) : |t| - s < x \}$ (see Figure \ref{captionW}) by \cite[Th. 5.1.6]{duistermaat-FIOs}. This implies that $u_0^\rightarrow = - u_0^\leftarrow $ in $W $. Since the wave front sets of these terms do not overlap, they must both be smooth in $W$ for this to hold. In $W \cap (0,\delta) \times \mathbb{R}$, they then reduce into $u_0^\rightarrow(x,t) = F_0(t-x)$ and $u_0^\leftarrow(x,t) = G_0(t+x)$, where $F_0$ and $G_0$ are smooth. In the coordinates $z_0 = t-x$ and $z_1 = t+x$, this reads $u_0^\rightarrow(z_0,z_1) = F_0(z_0)$ and $u_0^\leftarrow(z_0,z_1) = G_0(z_1)$. Setting $F_0(z_0) = - G_0(z_1)$ in $W \cap (0,\delta) \times \mathbb{R}$ implies $F_0(z_0) = C = - G_0(z_1)$ there. We can assume $C=0$ by redefining the functions $F_0 $ and $G_0 $. Indeed, the opposing constants $\pm C$ may be added to them without changing $u_0$.

nodes.name: Left-moving part vanishes in X
nodes.statement_short: Invariance along rays gives $u_0^\leftarrow=0$ in $X$
nodes.statement: With this choice, $u_0^\leftarrow = 0$ in $W \cap (0,\delta) \times \mathbb{R}$ and the invariance of $G_0(t+x)$ along the rays \[ R_c = \{ (x,t) \in (-\infty,\delta) \times \mathbb{R} : t + x =c\}, c \in \mathbb{R}, \] implies that $u_0^\leftarrow$ vanishes in \[ X:= \cup \{ R_c : c \in \mathbb{R}, \ R_c \cap W \neq \emptyset\} = \{ (x,t) \in (-\infty,\delta) \times \mathbb{R} : -x-s < t < 2 \delta + s -x \}. \] This set is shown in Figure \ref{captionX}.

nodes.name: Uniqueness in wedge V
nodes.statement_short: By Duistermaat Th. 5.1.6 the Cauchy solution is unique in the wedge $V$
nodes.statement: By \cite[Th. 5.1.6]{duistermaat-FIOs}, the solution to the Cauchy problem is unique in the wedge \[ V = \{ (x,t) \in (-\infty,\delta) {\times \mathbb{R}} : x < -|t| + \delta\}. \] This set is shown in Figure \ref{captionV}.

nodes.name: Explicit form in V and X
nodes.statement_short: Identify $u_0=(-1)^\mu\rho_-^*f^{(-\mu)}$ in $V\cup X_{t>0}$
nodes.statement: In our case, that solution is the function $(-1)^\mu \rho^*_- f^{(-\mu)} $. Hence, $u_0 = (-1)^\mu \rho^*_- f$ in $V$. This means that $u_0^\rightarrow= (-1)^\mu \rho^*_- f^{(-\mu)} $ and $u_0^\leftarrow = 0$ in $V$. On the other hand, $u_0^\rightarrow= \rho^*_- F_0$ holds in $(-\infty,\delta) \times \mathbb{R}$ and applying the invariance of $\rho^*_- F_0$ along the rays $x-t =c$, we deduce that $u_0^\rightarrow =(-1)^\mu \rho^*_- f^{(-\mu)} $ holds in \[ X_{t > 0} := \{ (x,t) \in X : t > 0 \} \] too. Indeed, the rays from $V \cap X$ fill $X_{t > 0}$ and we obtain the extension of $u_0^\rightarrow = (-1)^\mu \rho^*_- f^{(-\mu)} $ from $V \cap X$ to this set by the invariance. Since we already know that $u_0^\leftarrow$ vanishes in $X$, we conclude that $u_0 = (-1)^\mu \rho^*_- f^{(-\mu)} $ does not only hold in $V$ but also in $V \cup X_{t >0}$.

nodes.name: Extension to W
nodes.statement_short: Recall $u_0$ vanishes in $W$, extending the identity
nodes.statement: Recall that by \cite[Th. 5.1.6.]{duistermaat-FIOs} the wave $u_0$ vanishes in $W \supset (0,\infty) \times \{0\}$. This further extends the identity $u_0 = (-1)^\mu \rho^*_- f^{(-\mu)} $ to $V \cup X_{t >0} \cup W$.

nodes.name: Cut off and read off boundary data
nodes.statement_short: Cut off below $W$ and obtain $\partial_x^\mu u|_{x=0}=f$ for $t<2\delta+s$
nodes.statement: Considering $u_0$ as a distribution in $\mathcal{D}'((0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R})$, we may cut off everything below $W \cap (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}$ without conflicting $\square_A u_0 = 0$. Indeed, $\square_A u = 0$ in $(0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}$ for $u := \chi u_0$, where $\chi \in C^\infty$ satisfies $\chi|_{t>-s/4} = 1$ and $\chi|_{t<-s/2} = 0$. Moreover, $u$ vanishes in $(0,\infty) \times (-\infty,0)$ since $u_0 = 0$ in $W$ and $\chi$ cuts off everything below it in $(0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}$. As a conclusion, the identity $u = (-1)^\mu \rho^*_- f^{(-\mu)} $ holds in \[ V \cup X_{t >0} \cup W \cup \ker \chi . \] This set contains an open neighbourhood of $\{0\} \times (-\infty, 2 \delta + s)$ and hence \[ \partial^\mu_x u|_{x=0} = \partial^\mu_x ( (-1)^\mu \rho^*_- f^{(-\mu)} )|_{x=0} = f \] for $t<2 \delta + s$.

nodes.name: Independence of s and linearity
nodes.statement_short: Independence of $s$ and linearity are inherited from the Cauchy problem
nodes.statement: Finally, we note that the element $u=u_f$ above does not change if we choose different \\ $s \in (0,\min \operatorname{supp}(f))$. Indeed, the Cauchy problem \eqref{cauchy1}-\eqref{cauchy3}, which was used to generate $u$, remain the same. Moreover, the linearity of $u$ in $f$ is also inherited from the Cauchy problem.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of solutions
nodes.statement: Let $f \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})$ be supported in $(t_0,\infty)$. Let $u_1,u_2 \in \mathcal{D}_{\Sigma}'(\mathbb{R}^2) $ be two solutions to (\ref{ibvp1})-(\ref{ibvp4}). Then $u_1 = u_2 $ in $(0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.3
nodes.statement: Throughout the proof, we may assume that $t_0 = 0$. Define $v = u_1- u_2$. Then $v$ obeys \eqref{ibvp1}-\eqref{ibvp4} with $0$ substituted for $f$. Moreover, $v$ vanishes in $\{ (x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R} : t < x \}$ by \cite[Th. 5.1.6]{duistermaat-FIOs} and the fact that $v=0$ in $(0,\infty) \times (-\infty,0)$. Let us first assume that $v \in C^\infty ([0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R})$. Then we may consider the energy $E: [0,\infty) \to [0,\infty)$, \[ E(t) := \frac{1}{2} \int_0^t |\nabla_{x,t}v(x,t)|^2 A(x) d x = \frac{1}{2} \int_0^t [ (\partial_t v(x,t))^2 + (\partial_x v(x,t))^2 ]A (x) d x \] over $x$ in the expanding interval $(0,t)$. The derivative of $E(t)$ is \begin{align} E'(t) = \int_0^t [ \partial_t v(x,t) \partial_t^2 v(x,t) + \partial_x v(x,t) \partial_t \partial_x v(x,t) ] A(x) dx \\+ \frac{1}{2} [ (\partial_t v(t,t))^2 + (\partial_x v(t,t))^2 ] A (t). \end{align} The latter term must be zero since $v$ is smooth and vanishes on $\{ (x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R} : t < x \}$. In the first term, we integrate by parts. This gives \begin{align} E'(t) = \int_0^t \partial_t v(x,t) ( \square_A v(x,t) ) A(x)dx \\ +A(t) \partial_t v(t,t) \partial_x v(t,t) - A(0) \partial_t v(0,t) \partial_x v(0,t) \end{align} The first term vanishes since $ \square_A v = 0 $ in $(0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}$. The middle term is zero as $v$ is smooth and vanishes in $\{ (x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R} : t < x \}$. For the last term, we notice that {it} is zero as either $\partial_t v(0,t) = \partial_t ( v(0,t) ) $ or $\partial_x v(0,t) $ {vanishes} due to smoothness and $\partial^\mu v|_{x=0} =0$. Thus, $E'(t) = 0$. That is; the energy is conserved and we deduce $E(t) = E(0) = 0$. It is easy to check that this happens if and only if $v$ is constant in $\{ (x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R} : x< t \} $. Further, this constant is zero by the smoothness and $v(t,t)= 0$. In summary, $v$ is a smooth function that vanishes in $\{ (x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R} : t < x \}$ and $\{ (x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R} : x < t \}$. Therefore, it must be zero in $(0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}$. That is, $u_1 = u_2$ in $(0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}$. As shown above, the claim follows if $v = u_1 - u_2 $ is smooth in $[0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}$. Let us show that this indeed holds. Since $v = u_1 - u_2 \in \mathcal{D}_\Sigma' (\mathbb{R}^2) - \mathcal{D}_\Sigma' (\mathbb{R}^2) = \mathcal{D}_\Sigma' (\mathbb{R}^2) $, we have a well-defined boundary value \[ \partial_x^\mu v|_{x=0} = \partial_x^\mu u_1|_{x=0} - \partial_x^\mu u_2|_{x=0} = 0 \] which is obviously smooth. It suffices to show that $v \in C^\infty( (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R})$ (see Lemma \ref{ooiiqweh} below). For the rest of the proof, we consider $v$ as a distribution in $\mathcal{D}'( (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R})$. We split $v$ microlocally into $v = v^\rightarrow + v^\leftarrow $, where \begin{align} &WF( v^\rightarrow ) \subset \Sigma^\rightarrow := \{ (x,t,-\xi,\xi) : \xi \in \dot {\mathbb{R}} \}, \\ &WF( v^\leftarrow ) \subset \Sigma^\leftarrow := \{ (x,t,\xi,\xi) : \xi \in \dot {\mathbb{R}} \}. \end{align} By the propagation of singularities, these wave fronts are invariant in the canonical symplectic flows in $\Sigma^{\leftarrow}$ and $\Sigma^{\leftarrow}$ inherited from $\Sigma$. Recall that $v=0$ in $Q:= \{ (x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R} : t < x \} $. As the wave front sets of $v^\rightarrow$ and $ v^\leftarrow$ do not overlap, its must be that $v^\rightarrow$ and $ v^\leftarrow$ are smooth in $Q$. As every orbit (null bicharacteristic) in $\Sigma^{\leftarrow}$ reaches $Q \times \dot {\mathbb{R}}^2$, the component $v^\leftarrow$ is smooth in the whole $(0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}$ by the propagation of singularities. Using the fact that $\square_A = \square = \frac{1}{4} \partial_{z_+ } \partial_{z_-}$ in $(0,\delta) \times \mathbb{R}$ in the coordinates $z_\pm = t \pm x$, one can show that $v^\rightarrow(x,t) \equiv F(t-x)$, $F \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})$ is the general form of a wave in $(0,\delta) \times \mathbb{R}$ propagating in $\Sigma^\rightarrow$. Above, $F(t-x)$ stands for $\phi \mapsto \int F (s) \phi(x,s+x) ds dx$, $ \phi \in C^\infty_c $ in the sense of distributions. We have \[ 0 = \partial_x^\mu v|_{x= 0} = \partial_x^\mu \underbrace{v^\rightarrow}_{=F(t-x)} |_{x= 0}+ \underbrace{v^\leftarrow}_{\in C^\infty} |_{x= 0} \equiv (-1)^\mu F^{(\mu)} \mod C^\infty. \] Hence $v^\rightarrow \in C^\infty( (0,\delta) \times \mathbb{R})$ and therefore $v^\rightarrow \in C^\infty( (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R})$ by the propagation of singularities. In conclusion, $v = v^\rightarrow + v^\leftarrow \in C^\infty( (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R})+C^\infty( (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}) \subset C^\infty( (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R})$. This finishes the proof.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.4
nodes.statement: Let us deduce the claim in the case $\alpha = 0$. The general claim follows by replacing $v$ with $\partial_{x,t}^\alpha v$. Since $v$ is continuous in $(0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}$, the function $v_\epsilon(x,t) := v(x+\epsilon,t) $ is well defined pointwise on $(-\epsilon,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}$. Moreover, $v_\epsilon|_{x=0} (t) = v(\epsilon,t)$ pointwise. For $0 < \epsilon < \delta $, $v_\epsilon $ obeys the wave equation $\square v_\epsilon = 0$ in $(-\epsilon, \delta- \epsilon) \times \mathbb{R} $. Moreover, the wave has smooth Cauchy data on the surface $x=0$. Thus, \[ v_\epsilon(x,t) = F_\epsilon( x-t) + G_\epsilon( x+t) \] near the Cauchy surface for some smooth $F_\epsilon,G_\epsilon$ determined by the data. Moreover, \[ v_{\epsilon}(x,t) =v_{\epsilon'} (x+ \epsilon-\epsilon',t) \] so we may write \begin{align} F_\epsilon( r ) = F ( r + \epsilon ) \quad \quad G_\epsilon( r ) = G ( r + \epsilon ) \end{align} for some $F,G \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}) $. Hence, the pointwise limit \[ \lim_{\epsilon \to 0+} ( v_\epsilon|_{x=0} (t) )= \lim_{\epsilon \to 0+} v(\epsilon,t) = F(-t) + G(t) \] from the right exists and is smooth. The convergence is in fact uniform for $t $ in a compact set. It is easy to check that $v_\epsilon$ converges in $\mathcal{D}'_\Sigma(\mathbb{R}^2)$ to $v$. As the boundary restriction is continuous on $\mathcal{D}'_\Sigma (\mathbb{R}^2)$, the limit $ \lim_{\epsilon \to 0} ( v_\epsilon|_{x=0} ) $ in $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}) $ exists and equals to $v|_{x=0}$. This is the weak limit. Recall that also the pointwise limit exists. Moreover, the convergence to it is uniform in compact sets. Hence, the pointwise limit matches with the weak limit.
nodes.statement_short: Translate $v$ inward, write it via d'Alembert's formula near the boundary, and match the pointwise and distributional limits.

nodes.name: Inward translates
nodes.statement_short: Define the translates $v_\epsilon(x,t)=v(x+\epsilon,t)$
nodes.statement: Since $v$ is continuous in $(0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}$, the function $v_\epsilon(x,t) := v(x+\epsilon,t) $ is well defined pointwise on $(-\epsilon,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}$. Moreover, $v_\epsilon|_{x=0} (t) = v(\epsilon,t)$ pointwise.

nodes.name: d'Alembert form of translates
nodes.statement_short: Each $v_\epsilon$ is $F_\epsilon(x-t)+G_\epsilon(x+t)$ near $x=0$
nodes.statement: For $0 < \epsilon < \delta $, $v_\epsilon $ obeys the wave equation $\square v_\epsilon = 0$ in $(-\epsilon, \delta- \epsilon) \times \mathbb{R} $. Moreover, the wave has smooth Cauchy data on the surface $x=0$. Thus, \[ v_\epsilon(x,t) = F_\epsilon( x-t) + G_\epsilon( x+t) \] near the Cauchy surface for some smooth $F_\epsilon,G_\epsilon$ determined by the data.

nodes.name: Common profiles F, G
nodes.statement_short: Translates share profiles $F,G$
nodes.statement: Moreover, \[ v_{\epsilon}(x,t) =v_{\epsilon'} (x+ \epsilon-\epsilon',t) \] so we may write \begin{align} F_\epsilon( r ) = F ( r + \epsilon ) \quad \quad G_\epsilon( r ) = G ( r + \epsilon ) \end{align} for some $F,G \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}) $.

nodes.name: Equation (3.32)
nodes.statement: F_\epsilon( r ) = F ( r + \epsilon ) \quad \quad G_\epsilon( r ) = G ( r + \epsilon )

nodes.name: Pointwise limit exists
nodes.statement_short: The pointwise boundary limit $F(-t)+G(t)$ exists, locally uniformly
nodes.statement: Hence, the pointwise limit \[ \lim_{\epsilon \to 0+} ( v_\epsilon|_{x=0} (t) )= \lim_{\epsilon \to 0+} v(\epsilon,t) = F(-t) + G(t) \] from the right exists and is smooth. The convergence is in fact uniform for $t $ in a compact set.

nodes.name: Weak limit
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of the boundary restriction on $\mathcal{D}'_\Sigma$ gives the weak limit $v|_{x=0}$
nodes.statement: It is easy to check that $v_\epsilon$ converges in $\mathcal{D}'_\Sigma(\mathbb{R}^2)$ to $v$. As the boundary restriction is continuous on $\mathcal{D}'_\Sigma (\mathbb{R}^2)$, the limit $ \lim_{\epsilon \to 0} ( v_\epsilon|_{x=0} ) $ in $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}) $ exists and equals to $v|_{x=0}$. This is the weak limit.

nodes.name: Limits agree
nodes.statement_short: Uniform pointwise convergence makes the two limits agree
nodes.statement: Recall that also the pointwise limit exists. Moreover, the convergence to it is uniform in compact sets. Hence, the pointwise limit matches with the weak limit.

nodes.name: Dirichlet-to-Neumann and Neumann-to-Dirichlet operators
nodes.statement: Let $$\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})_{+} := \{ f \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}) : \text{supp} (f) \subset (t_0,\infty), \ \text{for some} \ t_0 \in \mathbb{R} \}.$$ We define \[ \Lambda_{\text{DN}} : \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})_{+} \to \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})_{+}, \quad \Lambda_{\text{DN}} (f) := \partial_x u |_{x=0}, \] where $u \in \mathcal{D}_\Sigma'(\mathbb{R}^2)$ satisfies the conditions (\ref{ibvp1}-\ref{ibvp4}) for $t_0 < \inf \text{supp} (f)$, $\mu=0$ and $f$ as the Dirichlet boundary value. Analogously, we define \[ \Lambda_{\text{ND}} : \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})_{+} \to \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})_{+}, \quad \Lambda_{\text{ND}} (f) := u |_{x=0}, \] where $u \in \mathcal{D}_\Sigma'(\mathbb{R}^2)$ satisfies the conditions (\ref{ibvp1}-\ref{ibvp4}) for $t_0 < \inf \text{supp} (f)$, $\mu=1$ and $f$ as the Neumann boundary value. We call $\Lambda_{DN}$ and $\Lambda_{ND}$ the Dirichlet-to-Neumann (DN) map and Neumann-to-Dirichlet (ND) map, respectively. These maps are continuous on $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})_{t_0} := \{ f \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}) : \text{supp} (f) \subset (t_0,\infty) \}$ for a fixed $t_0 \in \mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: DN map sends Dirichlet data to Neumann trace and ND map sends Neumann data to Dirichlet trace of the IBVP solution.
nodes.label: DN-def

nodes.name: Cut-off chi in Section 4
nodes.statement: Let $\chi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a smooth function such that $\text{supp}(\chi) \subset (0,\infty) $ and $\chi |_{[\delta,\infty)}=1$ for some $\delta >0$.

nodes.name: Wave operator square_A (Section 4)
nodes.statement: Denote by $\square_A $ the second order differential operator \begin{equation} \square_A v(t,x) := \partial_t^2v(t,x) - \frac{1}{A(x)} \partial_x ( A(x) \partial_x v(x,t)). \end{equation} where $A \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ is admissible (cf. Definition~\ref{def:admissible}).

nodes.name: Wave operator (4.1)
nodes.statement: \square_A v(t,x) := \partial_t^2v(t,x) - \frac{1}{A(x)} \partial_x ( A(x) \partial_x v(x,t)).
nodes.label: def-wave-op

nodes.name: White-noise wave u_omega
nodes.statement: Given $\omega\in \mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R})$, we let $u=u_\omega \in \mathcal{D}_\Sigma' (\mathbb{R}^2) \subset \mathcal{D}' ((0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R})$ solve \begin{align} & \square_A u(x,t) = 0, && \text{for} \quad (x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R} , \\ & \partial_x u |_{x=0} (t) = \chi (t) \omega (t), &&\text{for} \quad t \in \mathbb{R}, \\ & u (x,t)= 0, &&\text{for} \quad (x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times ( - \infty, 0) . \end{align}

nodes.name: White-noise IBVP (4.2)-(4.4)
nodes.statement: & \square_A u(x,t) = 0, && \text{for} \quad (x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R} ,\\ & \partial_x u |_{x=0} (t) = \chi (t) \omega (t), &&\text{for} \quad t \in \mathbb{R},\\ & u (x,t)= 0, &&\text{for} \quad (x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times ( - \infty, 0) .
nodes.label: eq:wave-u

nodes.name: Time-reversed wave tilde u_phi
nodes.statement: For $\phi \in C^\infty_c(\mathbb{R})$, let $\tilde{u} = \tilde{u}_\phi \in C^\infty ( [0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R})$ be a solution to the time-reversed initial-boundary value problem \begin{align} & \square_A \tilde{u}(x,t) = 0, && \text{for} \quad (x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R} , \\ & \partial_x \tilde{u} |_{x=0} (t) = \phi(t), &&\text{for} \quad t \in \mathbb{R}, \\ & \tilde{u} (x,t)= 0, &&\text{for} \quad (x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times ( t_0 , \infty ) . \end{align} where $t_0 > \max \text{supp}(\phi) $.

nodes.name: Time-reversed IBVP (4.5)-(4.7)
nodes.statement: & \square_A \tilde{u}(x,t) = 0, && \text{for} \quad (x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R} ,\\ & \partial_x \tilde{u} |_{x=0} (t) = \phi(t), &&\text{for} \quad t \in \mathbb{R},\\ & \tilde{u} (x,t)= 0, &&\text{for} \quad (x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times ( t_0 , \infty ) .
nodes.label: tr:eq:wave-u

nodes.name: Well-posedness of the time-reversed problem
nodes.statement: Existence and uniqueness in $(0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R}$ for $\tilde{u}$ follows from the theory developed for the forwards propagating solution $u$.

nodes.name: Time-reversal relation
nodes.statement: One checks that the relation between them is \begin{equation} \tilde{u}_\phi (x,t) = u_{ \psi } (x,t_0-t), \end{equation} where $\psi (t) := \phi(t_0 - t)$.

nodes.name: Time-reversal relation (4.8)
nodes.statement: \tilde{u}_\phi (x,t) = u_{ \psi } (x,t_0-t),
nodes.label: rev-fut

nodes.name: Time-reversed Neumann-to-Dirichlet map
nodes.statement: We define the time-reversed Neumann-to-Dirichlet map $\tilde\Lambda_{ND} : C^\infty_c (\mathbb{R}) \to C^\infty( \mathbb{R})$ by $ \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi) = \tilde{u}_{ \phi }|_{x=0} $.

nodes.name: Duality between ND map and time-reversed ND map
nodes.statement: Let $A \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ be admissible. Let $f \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})$ be supported in $(0,\infty)$. Then, \begin{equation} \langle \Lambda_{ND} (f), \phi \rangle = \langle f , \tilde\Lambda_{ND} ( \phi ) \rangle, \end{equation} {for all $\phi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$.}
nodes.statement_short: The ND map and the time-reversed ND map are adjoint: $\langle \Lambda_{ND} f,\phi\rangle=\langle f,\tilde\Lambda_{ND}\phi\rangle$.
nodes.label: prop:integration-by-parts

nodes.name: Duality identity (4.9)
nodes.statement: \langle \Lambda_{ND} (f), \phi \rangle = \langle f , \tilde\Lambda_{ND} ( \phi ) \rangle,

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.1
nodes.statement: Let $\psi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ be a mollifier and denote $\psi_\varepsilon(t) = \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \psi ( \varepsilon t)$. For sufficiently small values of $\varepsilon >0 $, the smooth function $f_\varepsilon := \psi_\varepsilon * f $ is supported in $(0,\infty)$. Let us denote by $u_\varepsilon $ the smooth wave $u_{f_\varepsilon}$. A straightforward computation gives \begin{align} \langle \Lambda_{\text{ND}} (f_\varepsilon), \phi \rangle &= \int_{\mathbb{R}} u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) \phi (t) dt = \int_{\mathbb{R}} u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) A(0) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) dt \\ & {= - \int_{\mathbb{R}} \int_0^\infty \partial_x [ u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) A(x) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) ] dx dt + \int_{\mathbb{R}} \lim_{x \to \infty} \partial_x [ u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) A(x) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) ] dt} \\ &= - \int_{\mathbb{R}} \int_0^\infty \partial_x [ u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) A(x) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) ] dx dt + { \int_{\mathbb{R}} 0 dt } \\ &= -\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_0^\infty \bigg[ ( \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) ) A(x) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) + u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) \partial_x (A(x) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) ) \bigg] dx dt. \end{align} {where the identity \eqref{roqw13} is due to finite speed of propagation. Indeed, the wave $u_{\varepsilon} (x,t)$ has null Cauchy data on $(0,\infty) \times \{0\}$ and therefore vanishes in the wedge $\{(x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R} : |t| < x\}$. Further, } integration by parts in $x$ yields \begin{align} &\langle \Lambda_{\text{ND}} (f_\varepsilon), \phi \rangle = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \int_0^\infty \bigg[ \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) \partial_x ( A(x) \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) ) +( A(x) \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) ) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) \bigg] dx dt. \\ &+ \int_{\mathbb{R}} \bigg[ \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) + u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \bigg] dt \\ & = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \int_0^\infty \partial_x [ A(x) u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) ]dx dt. + \int_{\mathbb{R}} \bigg[ \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) + u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \bigg] dt \\ & = - \int_{\mathbb{R}} \underbrace{A(0)}_{=1} u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) dt. +\int_{\mathbb{R}} \bigg[ \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) + u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \bigg] dt \\ & = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) dt = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) f_\varepsilon(t) dt = \langle f_\varepsilon, \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi) \rangle. \end{align} By taking the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$ and applying continuity of $\Lambda_{\text{ND}}$ on $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})_{0} := \{ f \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}) : \text{supp} (f) \subset (0,\infty) \}$, we conclude \[ \langle \Lambda_{\text{ND}} ( f ), \phi \rangle = \langle f , \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi) \rangle. \]
nodes.statement_short: Mollify $f$, integrate by parts in $x$ using the Neumann data of both waves and finite speed of propagation, then let $\varepsilon\to0$.

nodes.name: Mollified data
nodes.statement_short: Mollify $f$ to get smooth waves $u_\varepsilon$
nodes.statement: Let $\psi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ be a mollifier and denote $\psi_\varepsilon(t) = \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \psi ( \varepsilon t)$. For sufficiently small values of $\varepsilon >0 $, the smooth function $f_\varepsilon := \psi_\varepsilon * f $ is supported in $(0,\infty)$. Let us denote by $u_\varepsilon $ the smooth wave $u_{f_\varepsilon}$.

nodes.name: First integration
nodes.statement_short: Write the pairing as a boundary term and integrate in $x$; finite speed kills the term at infinity
nodes.statement: A straightforward computation gives \begin{align} \langle \Lambda_{\text{ND}} (f_\varepsilon), \phi \rangle &= \int_{\mathbb{R}} u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) \phi (t) dt = \int_{\mathbb{R}} u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) A(0) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) dt \\ & {= - \int_{\mathbb{R}} \int_0^\infty \partial_x [ u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) A(x) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) ] dx dt + \int_{\mathbb{R}} \lim_{x \to \infty} \partial_x [ u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) A(x) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) ] dt} \\ &= - \int_{\mathbb{R}} \int_0^\infty \partial_x [ u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) A(x) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) ] dx dt + { \int_{\mathbb{R}} 0 dt } \\ &= -\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_0^\infty \bigg[ ( \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) ) A(x) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) + u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) \partial_x (A(x) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) ) \bigg] dx dt. \end{align} {where the identity \eqref{roqw13} is due to finite speed of propagation. Indeed, the wave $u_{\varepsilon} (x,t)$ has null Cauchy data on $(0,\infty) \times \{0\}$ and therefore vanishes in the wedge $\{(x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R} : |t| < x\}$.

nodes.name: Equation (4.10)
nodes.statement: \langle \Lambda_{\text{ND}} (f_\varepsilon), \phi \rangle &= \int_{\mathbb{R}} u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) \phi (t) dt = \int_{\mathbb{R}} u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) A(0) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) dt \\ & {= - \int_{\mathbb{R}} \int_0^\infty \partial_x [ u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) A(x) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) ] dx dt + \int_{\mathbb{R}} \lim_{x \to \infty} \partial_x [ u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) A(x) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) ] dt} \\ &= - \int_{\mathbb{R}} \int_0^\infty \partial_x [ u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) A(x) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) ] dx dt + { \int_{\mathbb{R}} 0 dt } \\ &= -\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_0^\infty \bigg[ ( \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) ) A(x) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) + u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) \partial_x (A(x) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) ) \bigg] dx dt.
nodes.label: roqw13

nodes.name: Integration by parts
nodes.statement_short: Integrate by parts again to reach $\langle f_\varepsilon,\tilde\Lambda_{ND}\phi\rangle$
nodes.statement: Further, } integration by parts in $x$ yields \begin{align} &\langle \Lambda_{\text{ND}} (f_\varepsilon), \phi \rangle = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \int_0^\infty \bigg[ \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) \partial_x ( A(x) \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) ) +( A(x) \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) ) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) \bigg] dx dt. \\ &+ \int_{\mathbb{R}} \bigg[ \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) + u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \bigg] dt \\ & = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \int_0^\infty \partial_x [ A(x) u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) ]dx dt. + \int_{\mathbb{R}} \bigg[ \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) + u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \bigg] dt \\ & = - \int_{\mathbb{R}} \underbrace{A(0)}_{=1} u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) dt. +\int_{\mathbb{R}} \bigg[ \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) + u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \bigg] dt \\ & = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) dt = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) f_\varepsilon(t) dt = \langle f_\varepsilon, \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi) \rangle. \end{align}

nodes.name: Equation (4.14)
nodes.statement: &\langle \Lambda_{\text{ND}} (f_\varepsilon), \phi \rangle = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \int_0^\infty \bigg[ \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) \partial_x ( A(x) \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) ) +( A(x) \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) ) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) \bigg] dx dt. \\ &+ \int_{\mathbb{R}} \bigg[ \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) + u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \bigg] dt \\ & = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \int_0^\infty \partial_x [ A(x) u_{\varepsilon} (x,t) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (x,t) ]dx dt. + \int_{\mathbb{R}} \bigg[ \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) + u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \bigg] dt \\ & = - \int_{\mathbb{R}} \underbrace{A(0)}_{=1} u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) dt. +\int_{\mathbb{R}} \bigg[ \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) + u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) \partial_x \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \bigg] dt \\ & = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) \partial_x u_{\varepsilon} (0,t) dt = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \tilde{u}_{\phi} (0,t) f_\varepsilon(t) dt = \langle f_\varepsilon, \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi) \rangle.

nodes.name: Remove the mollifier
nodes.statement_short: Let $\varepsilon\to0$ using continuity of $\Lambda_{ND}$
nodes.statement: By taking the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$ and applying continuity of $\Lambda_{\text{ND}}$ on $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})_{0} := \{ f \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}) : \text{supp} (f) \subset (0,\infty) \}$, we conclude \[ \langle \Lambda_{\text{ND}} ( f ), \phi \rangle = \langle f , \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi) \rangle. \]

nodes.name: Correlation operator C_T
nodes.statement: Denote by $\tau_s$ the time-shift $\tau_s(t) = t+s$. Let $T>0$ and let $A$ be admissible. The correlation operator $C_T : {\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R} ) \times }C^\infty_c ( \mathbb{R}) \to \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})$ is defined by \begin{equation} \langle C_T (\omega, \phi ), \psi \rangle := \frac1T\int_0^T \langle \tau_s^* \Lambda_{\text{ND}} (\chi \omega ), \phi \rangle \langle \tau_s^* \omega, \psi \rangle ds \end{equation} where $\phi, \psi \in C^\infty_c(\mathbb{R})$. { We shall omit the parameter $\omega$ and denote $C_T (\phi):= C_T(\omega,\phi) \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})$ whenever there is no danger of confusion. } {The correlation operator is inherently stochastic and may be regarded as an operator-valued random variable. Alternatively, via Schwartz’s kernel theorem, it can be viewed as a $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}^2)$-valued random variable. }
nodes.statement_short: $C_T$ time-averages over $[0,T]$ the product of shifted ND output tested with $\phi$ and shifted noise tested with $\psi$.

nodes.name: Correlation operator (4.19)
nodes.statement: \langle C_T (\omega, \phi ), \psi \rangle := \frac1T\int_0^T \langle \tau_s^* \Lambda_{\text{ND}} (\chi \omega ), \phi \rangle \langle \tau_s^* \omega, \psi \rangle ds
nodes.label: eq:correlation-function-def

nodes.name: Expected correlation converges to time-reversed ND map
nodes.statement: Let $\phi , \psi \in C^\infty_c(\mathbb{R})$. Then \[ \lim_{T \to \infty} \mathbb{E} \langle C_T ( \phi) , \psi \rangle = \langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ) , \psi \rangle. \]
nodes.label: weaklemma

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.3
nodes.statement: Denote \begin{equation} X_s := \langle \tau_s^* \Lambda_{\text{ND}} (\chi \omega ), \phi \rangle, \qquad Y_s := \langle \tau_s^* \omega, \psi \rangle. \end{equation} Proposition \ref{prop:integration-by-parts} implies that $ X_s = \langle \omega , \tilde\phi \rangle$ where $ \tilde\phi := \chi \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\tau_{-s}^* \phi ) \in C^\infty_c(\mathbb{R}) \subset \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}). $ Similarly, $Y_s = \langle \omega, \tilde\psi \rangle$ for $\tilde\psi:= \tau_{-s}^* \psi \in C^\infty_c(\mathbb{R}) \subset \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}) $. By the isometry \eqref{itolike}, \[ \mathbb{E} (X_s Y_s) = \langle \tilde\phi , \tilde\psi \rangle =\langle \chi \tilde\Lambda_{ND} ( \tau_{-s}^*\phi ), \tau_{-s}^*\psi \rangle . \] It is easy to check that $\tilde\Lambda_{ND} ( \tau_{-s}^* \phi ) = \tau_{-s}^*\tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi)$. Substituting this in the previous equation leads to \begin{align} \mathbb{E} (X_s Y_s) =\langle \chi \tau_{-s}^* \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ) , \tau_{-s}^* \psi \rangle = \langle ( \tau_{s}^* \chi ) \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ) , \psi \rangle. \end{align} Moreover, by Hölder's inequality and the isometry \eqref{itolike}, \[ \mathbb{E} |X_s Y_s| \leq \| X_s \|_{L^2(\mathbb{P})} \| Y_s \|_{L^2(\mathbb{P})} = \| \tilde\phi \|_{L^2(\mathbb{R})} \| \tilde\psi \|_{L^2(\mathbb{R})} < \infty. \] Hence, $\frac{1}{T} \int_0^T \mathbb{E} |X_s Y_s| ds < \infty.$ By Fubini's theorem, \[ \mathbb{E} \langle C_T ( \phi) ,\psi \rangle = \mathbb{E} \frac{1}{T} \int_0^T X_s Y_s ds = \frac{1}{T} \int_0^T \mathbb{E} (X_s Y_s) ds . \] Applying \eqref{k10} we obtain \begin{align} \mathbb{E} \langle C_T ( \phi) ,\psi \rangle = \frac{1}{T} \int_0^T \langle ( \tau_{s}^* \chi ) \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ) , \psi \rangle ds = \langle \chi_T \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ) , \psi \rangle , \end{align} where \[ \chi_T(t) := \frac{1}{T} \int_0^T \chi (t+s) ds . \] We have \begin{align} &|1- \chi_T(t) | = \left| \frac{1}{T} \int_0^T (1-\chi(t+s)) ds \right| = \left| \frac{1}{T} \int_0^{\min\{T,\delta-t\}} (1-\chi(t+s)) ds \right| \\ & \leq \frac{1}{T} \int_0^{\min\{T,\delta-t\}} \left| (1-\chi(t+s)) \right|ds \leq \frac{1}{T} \int_0^{\delta-t} (1+\|\chi\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R})}) ds = \frac{ (1+\|\chi\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R})}) (\delta - t)}{T}, \end{align} which implies that $\chi_T(t) \to 1$ pointwise as $T$ grows. Moreover, \[ | \chi_T(t) | \leq \left| \frac{1}{T} \int_0^T \chi(t+s) ds \right| \leq \frac{1}{T} \int_0^T \left| \chi(t+s) \right|ds \leq \frac{1}{T} \int_0^T \| \chi \|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R})} ds = \| \chi \|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R})}. \] Consequently, $ \chi_T \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ) \psi \to \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ) \psi $ pointwise and $| \chi_T \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ) \psi |$ is dominated by the integrable function $ \| \chi \|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R})} | \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ) \psi| $.
