nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.4
nodes.statement: Denote \begin{equation} X_s := \langle \tau_s^* \Lambda_{\text{ND}} (\chi \omega ), \phi \rangle, \qquad Y_s := \langle \tau_s^* \omega, \psi \rangle. \end{equation} It follows from the definition of white noise measure that $ \langle \omega, \varphi \rangle $ is a Gaussian random variable with zero mean for every $\varphi \in \mathcal{S}$. Applying Proposition \ref{prop:integration-by-parts}, we get that $ X_s = \langle \omega , \tilde\phi_s \rangle$ where $ \tilde\phi_s := \chi \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi \circ \tau_{-s} ) \in C^\infty_c(\mathbb{R}) \subset \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}). $ Hence, $X_s$ is a Gaussian random variable with zero mean. Similarly, $Y_s = \langle \omega, \tilde\psi_s \rangle$ for $\tilde\psi_s:= \psi \circ \tau_{-s} \in C^\infty_c(\mathbb{R}) \subset \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}) $ so $Y_s$ is a Gaussian random variable with zero mean. According to Isserli's formula \cite{isserlis18_formul_produc_momen_coeff_any}, \begin{align} \mathbb{E}[&X_sY_sX_{r}Y_{r}] = \mathbb{E}[X_sY_s] \mathbb{E}[X_{r}Y_{r}] + \mathbb{E}[X_sX_{r}] \mathbb{E}[Y_sY_{r}] + \mathbb{E}[X_sY_{r}] \mathbb{E}[X_{r} Y_s]. \end{align} By the isometry \eqref{itolike}, \begin{align} \mathbb{E}[X_sY_sX_{r}Y_{r}] &= \langle \tilde\phi_s, \tilde\psi_s \rangle \langle \tilde\phi_{r}, \tilde\psi_{r} \rangle+\langle \tilde\phi_s, \tilde\phi_{r} \rangle \langle \tilde\psi_{s}, \tilde\psi_{r} \rangle+\langle \tilde\phi_s, \tilde\psi_{r} \rangle \langle \tilde\phi_{r}, \tilde\psi_{s} \rangle. \\ &= \langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} ( \tau_{-s}^* \phi ), \chi ( \tau_{-s}^* \psi ) \rangle \langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\tau_{-r} ^* \phi ), \chi (\tau_{-r}^* \psi ) \rangle \\ &+\langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\tau_{-s}^* \phi ), \chi^2 \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\tau_{-r}^* \phi ) \rangle \langle \tau_{-s}^* \psi , \tau_{-r}^* \psi \rangle \\ &+ \langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\tau_{-s}^*\phi ), \chi( \tau_{-r}^*\psi ) \rangle \langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} ( \tau_{-r}^*\phi ), \chi( \tau_{-s}^*\psi ) \rangle. \end{align} One checks that $ \tilde\Lambda_{ND} ( \tau_{-s}^* \phi ) = \tau_{-s}^* \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi) $. Similarly, $ \tilde\Lambda_{ND} ( \tau_{-r}^* \phi ) = \tau_{-r} ^*\tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi) $. Substituting this in the previous equation gives \begin{align} \mathbb{E}[X_sY_sX_{r}Y_{r}] &= \langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ), ( \tau_{s}^* \chi ) \psi \rangle \langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ), (\tau_{r}^* \chi ) \psi \rangle \\ &+\langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ), (\tau_{{s}}^* \chi )^2 \tau_{{s-r}}^* \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ) \rangle \langle \psi , \tau_{s-r}^*\psi \rangle \\ &+ \langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ), (\tau_s^* \chi ) (\tau_{s-r}^* \psi ) \rangle \langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ), (\tau_r^* \chi ) ( \tau_{r-s}^* \psi )\rangle. \end{align} Thus, \begin{align} \mathbb{E} \langle C_T (\phi ), \psi \rangle^2 &= \frac{1}{T^2} \int_0^T \int_0^T \mathbb{E}[X_sY_sX_{r}Y_{r}] ds dr \\ &= + \frac{1}{T^2} \int_0^T \int_0^T \langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ), (\tau_{s}^* \chi) \psi \rangle \langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ), (\tau_{r}^*\chi ) \psi \rangle ds dr \\ &+ \frac{1}{T^2} \int_0^T \int_0^T\langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ), (\tau_{{s}}^* \chi )^2 ( \tau_{{s-r}}^*\tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ) ) \rangle \langle \psi , \tau_{s-r}^*\psi \rangle ds dr \\ &+ \frac{1}{T^2} \int_0^T \int_0^T\langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ), (\tau_s^*\chi) \tau_{s-r}^*\psi \rangle \langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ), ( \tau_r^*\chi ) \tau_{r-s}^*\psi \rangle ds dr. \end{align} The first term on the right equals $ \langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ), \tilde\chi_T \psi \rangle \langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ), \tilde\chi_T \psi \rangle $, where $\tilde\chi_T (t) = \frac{1}{T} \int^T_0 \chi (t+s) ds $. The term converges {to} $ \langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ), \psi \rangle^2$ as $ T \to \infty$. The second term can be written in the form \begin{align} & \frac{1}{T^2} \int_0^T \int_0^{t_\psi} \langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ), (\tau_{{\tilde{s}+r}}^*\chi )^2 \tau_{{\tilde{s}}}^*\tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ) \rangle \langle \psi , \tau_{\tilde{s}}^* \psi \rangle d\tilde{s} dr , \end{align} where $t_\psi := \text{diam} ( \text{supp} ( \psi ) ) < \infty$ and $ \tilde{s} = s-r$. We would like to show that this converges to zero as $T \to \infty$. Since the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality implies $| \langle \psi , \tau_{\tilde{s}}^*\psi \rangle| \leq \| \psi \|^2_{L^2} < \infty$, the limit relies on the behaviour of $ \langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ), (\tau_{{\tilde{s}+r}}^*\chi )^2 \tau_{{\tilde{s}}}^*\tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ) \rangle $ as $r $ grows. It suffices to prove that \begin{equation} | \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi)(t) | \leq C e^{-C'|t|} , \quad \text{i.e.} \quad | \tilde{u}_\phi (0,t) | \leq C e^{-C'|t|} , \end{equation} for some $C,C'>0$. Before going into that, let us study the last term \eqref{isse43}. It reads \[ \frac{1}{T^2} \int_0^T \int_0^T\langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ), ( \tau_{\tilde{s}+r}^* \chi ) \tau_{\tilde{s}}^* \psi \rangle \langle \tilde\Lambda_{ND} (\phi ), (\tau_r^* \chi ) \tau_{-\tilde{s}}^* \psi \rangle d \tilde{s} dr. \] The supports of the test functions $ ( \tau_{\tilde{s}+r}^* \chi ) \tau_{\tilde{s}}^* \psi $ and $(\tau_r^* \chi ) \tau_{-\tilde{s}}^* \psi $ are shifted further as $\tilde{s}$ and $\tilde{r}$ grow. Hence, also this integral converges to $0$ provided the decay estimate \eqref{19q}. The estimate indeed holds, as shown in the lemma below. This finishes the proof.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.5
nodes.statement: Recall that the time-reversed wave is related to the standard one via $\tilde{u}_\phi (x,t) = u_{\psi} (x,t_0- t)$, where $ \psi (t) = \phi(t_0- t)$ and $t_0 > \max \text{supp} (\phi) $. Hence, it suffices to study the decay of $ u_{\psi}$ instead. According to Proposition \ref{1decay-pro}, \[ \abs{\tilde{u}_\phi (0,t) - c(t_0-t)}= \abs{u_\psi (0,t_0-t) - c(t_0-t)} \leq C e^{-C' (t_0-t)}. \] where $c(t) := -\frac{1}{A_\infty} \int_0^t \psi (s) ds = -\frac{1}{A_\infty}\int_0^t \phi (t_0- s) ds $. The function $c(t_0-t) $ vanishes for large $|t| $ by the assumption $\int_{\mathbb{R}} \phi (t) dt = 0$. Hence, \[ \abs{\tilde{u}_\phi (0,t) } \leq C e^{-C' (t_0-t)}. \] for such $t$. We need to show that there is a measurable $U \subset \mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R})$ with $\mathbb{P}(U) = 1$ such that $\Lambda_{1}(\chi \omega) \neq \Lambda_{2}(\chi \omega)$ for every $\omega \in U$. Consider test functions $\phi_k, \psi \in C^\infty_c (\mathbb{R})$, $k =1,2,3,\dots$ such that $\int \phi_k (x) dx = 0$. We shall fix $\phi_k$ more precisely later.

nodes.name: L^1 convergence
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 4.6 gives $L^1(\mathbb{P})$ convergence of the correlation differences

nodes.name: Almost sure subsequence
nodes.statement_short: Extract an a.s. convergent subsequence for $\phi_1$
nodes.statement: Recall that any sequence converging in $L^1 $ admits a sub-sequence that converges pointwise almost surely. Hence, there are increasing $T_{1j} $, $j=1,2,3,\dots$, such that $\langle C_{T_{1j}1}(\phi_1)-C_{T_{1j}2}(\phi_1) , \psi \rangle$ converges to $ \langle \tilde\Lambda_{1} (\phi_1 )-\tilde\Lambda_{2} (\phi_1 ), \psi \rangle$ pointwise almost surely. That is; there is a measurable set $U_1 \subset \mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R})$ such that $\mathbb{P} (U_1) = 1$ and \begin{equation} \lim_{j \to \infty} \langle C_{T_{1j}1}(\phi_1)-C_{T_{1j}2}(\phi_1) , \psi \rangle = \langle \tilde\Lambda_{1} (\phi_1 )-\tilde\Lambda_{2} (\phi_1 ), \psi \rangle \end{equation} at every $\omega \in U_1$.

nodes.name: Equation (4.43)
nodes.statement: \lim_{j \to \infty} \langle C_{T_{1j}1}(\phi_1)-C_{T_{1j}2}(\phi_1) , \psi \rangle = \langle \tilde\Lambda_{1} (\phi_1 )-\tilde\Lambda_{2} (\phi_1 ), \psi \rangle
nodes.label: eqp:991221

nodes.name: Diagonal subsequence
nodes.statement_short: Repeat for every $k$ and diagonalise to get one full-measure set $U$
nodes.statement: We can use the same argument to find an increasing subsequence $T_{2j}$ of $T_{1j}$ and measurable $U_2 \subset \mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R})$ such that $\mathbb{P} (U_2) = 1$ and \begin{equation} \lim_{j \to \infty} \langle C_{T_{2j}1}(\phi_2)-C_{T_{2j}2}(\phi_2) , \psi \rangle = \langle \tilde\Lambda_{1} (\phi_2 )-\tilde\Lambda_{2} (\phi_2 ), \psi \rangle \end{equation} at every $\omega \in U_2$. Moreover, we may assume $U_2 \subset U_1$ by taking intersection with $U_1$. Repeating this construction for every $k=1,2,3,\dots$ we obtain subsequences $(T_{kj})$, $k=1,2,3\dots$ and nested $U_1 \supset U_{2} \supset \cdots $ such that $\mathbb{P} (U_k) = 1$ and \begin{equation} \lim_{j \to \infty} \langle C_{T_{kj}1}(\phi_k)-C_{T_{kj}2}(\phi_k) , \psi \rangle = \langle \tilde\Lambda_{1} (\phi_k )-\tilde\Lambda_{2} (\phi_k ), \psi \rangle \end{equation} at every $\omega \in U_k$. Define $T_j := T_{jj}$ and $U := \cap_{k} U_k$. Then, $\mathbb{P} (U) =\lim_{k\to \infty} \mathbb{P} (U_k) = 1$ and \begin{equation} \lim_{j \to \infty} \langle C_{T_{j}1}(\phi_k)-C_{T_{j}2}(\phi_k) , \psi \rangle = \langle \tilde\Lambda_{1} (\phi_k )-\tilde\Lambda_{2} (\phi_k ), \psi \rangle \end{equation} for every $k=1,2,3,\dots$ and $\omega \in U$.

nodes.name: Equation (4.44)
nodes.statement: \lim_{j \to \infty} \langle C_{T_{2j}1}(\phi_2)-C_{T_{2j}2}(\phi_2) , \psi \rangle = \langle \tilde\Lambda_{1} (\phi_2 )-\tilde\Lambda_{2} (\phi_2 ), \psi \rangle
nodes.label: eqp:991222

nodes.name: Equation (4.45)
nodes.statement: \lim_{j \to \infty} \langle C_{T_{kj}1}(\phi_k)-C_{T_{kj}2}(\phi_k) , \psi \rangle = \langle \tilde\Lambda_{1} (\phi_k )-\tilde\Lambda_{2} (\phi_k ), \psi \rangle
nodes.label: eqp:991223

nodes.name: Equation (4.46)
nodes.statement: \lim_{j \to \infty} \langle C_{T_{j}1}(\phi_k)-C_{T_{j}2}(\phi_k) , \psi \rangle = \langle \tilde\Lambda_{1} (\phi_k )-\tilde\Lambda_{2} (\phi_k ), \psi \rangle
nodes.label: eqp:99122

nodes.name: Limit in k
nodes.statement_short: With $\phi_k=\varphi-\varphi(\cdot+k)$, the double limit recovers $\tilde\Lambda_1\varphi-\tilde\Lambda_2\varphi$
nodes.statement: Fix $\varphi \in C^\infty_c(\mathbb{R})$ and define the sequence $\phi_k \in C^\infty_c(\mathbb{R})$, $k=1,2,3,\dots$ by $\phi_k = \varphi - \varphi (x + k)$. Analogously to $\Lambda_\nu $ being continuous on $\mathcal{D}_{t_0}' (\mathbb{R})$, the operator $ \tilde\Lambda_{\nu}$ is continuous on the time-reversed domain $\tilde{\mathcal{D}}_{t_0}' (\mathbb{R}) := \{ f \in \mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R}) : \text{supp} (f) \subset (-\infty, t_0) \} $ and we have for every $\psi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ that \[ \lim_{k \to \infty } \langle \tilde\Lambda_{1} (\phi_k )-\tilde\Lambda_{2} (\phi_k ), \psi \rangle = \langle \tilde\Lambda_{1} (\varphi )-\tilde\Lambda_{2} (\varphi ), \psi \rangle \] at every $\omega \in U$. Moreover, the left hand side is \[ \lim_{k \to \infty } \lim_{j \to \infty } \langle C_{T_{j}1}(\phi_k)-C_{T_{j}2}(\phi_k) , \psi \rangle \] by \eqref{eqp:99122}. Thus, \[ \lim_{k \to \infty } \lim_{j \to \infty } \langle C_{T_{j}1}(\phi_k)-C_{T_{j}2}(\phi_k) , \psi \rangle = \langle \tilde\Lambda_{1} (\varphi )-\tilde\Lambda_{2} (\varphi ), \psi \rangle \] The test functions $\varphi , \psi \in C^\infty_c( \mathbb{R})$ above can be chosen freely.

nodes.name: Weighted energy E_{phi,g1,g2}
nodes.statement: For $\tau\in\mathbb{R}$, define the energy located in that interval at time $t=\tau$ by \begin{equation} \mathscr{E}_{\phi,g_1,g_2}(\tau) := \frac{1}{2} \int_0^\ell \left[ g_1(x)\big(\partial_t u(x,\tau) + \partial_x u(x,\tau)\big)^2 + g_2(x)\big(\partial_t u(x,\tau) - \partial_x u(x,\tau)\big)^2 \right] A(x) \,\mathrm{d}x \end{equation} where $u \in C^\infty ( [0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R})$ satisfies \begin{align} \square_A u &= 0, && x>0,\, t\in\mathbb{R}, \\ \partial_x u(0,t) &= \phi(t), && t\in\mathbb{R},\\ u(x,t) &= 0, && x>0,\, t<0, \end{align} and $\square_A$ is as defined in (\ref{def-wave-op}).

nodes.name: Derivation of the energy decay inequality
nodes.statement: Because everything is smooth and bounded, we can differentiate under the integral sign. We get \begin{align*} &\mathscr{E}_{\phi,g_1,g_2}'(\tau) = \int_0^\ell \left[ g_1 (\partial_t u + \partial_x u) (\partial_t^2 u + \partial_t\partial_x u) + g_2 (\partial_t u - \partial_x u) (\partial_t^2 u - \partial_t\partial_x u) \right] A \,\mathrm{d}x \\ \end{align*} Applying $\square_A u = 0$ yields \begin{align*} \mathscr{E}_{\phi,g_1,g_2}'(\tau) &= \int_0^\ell \Big[ g_1 (\partial_t u + \partial_x u) \Big(\partial_x^2 u + \frac{\partial_x A}{A} \partial_x u \\ &\qquad\quad + \partial_t\partial_x u\Big) + g_2 (\partial_t u - \partial_x u) \Big(\partial_x^2 u + \frac{\partial_x A}{A} \partial_x u - \partial_t\partial_x u \Big) \Big] A \,\mathrm{d}x. \\ &= \int_0^\ell \Big[ g_1 (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)(\partial_x^2 u + \partial_x \partial_t u) + g_1 (\partial_t u + \partial_x u) \frac{\partial_x A}{A} \partial_x u \\ &\qquad\quad + g_2 (\partial_t u - \partial_x u) (\partial_x^2 u - \partial_x \partial_t u) + g_2 (\partial_t u - \partial_x u) \frac{\partial_x A}{A} \partial_x u \Big] A \,\mathrm{d}x \\ &= \frac{1}{2} \int_0^\ell \Big[ g_1 \partial_x (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2 - g_2 \partial_x (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2 + \frac{\partial_x A}{A} \big(g_1 (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2 - g_2 (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2\big) \\ &\qquad\qquad - \frac{\partial_x A}{A} (g_1 - g_2) \big((\partial_t u)^2 - (\partial_x u)^2 \big) \Big] A \,\mathrm{d}x \\ &= \frac{1}{2} \int_0^\ell \Big[ g_1 \partial_x \big( A (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2 \big) - g_2 \partial_x \big( A (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2 \big) - \partial_x A (g_1 - g_2) \big( (\partial_t u)^2 - (\partial_x u)^2 \big) \Big] \,\mathrm{d}x. \\ \end{align*} Further, integrating by parts leads to \begin{multline} \mathscr{E}_{\phi,g_1,g_2}'(\tau) = \frac{1}{2} \intlim{0}{\ell} \Big[ g_1 A (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2 - g_2 A (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2 \Big] \\ + \frac{1}{2} \int_0^\ell \Big[ -\partial_x g_1 A (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2 + \partial_x g_2 A (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2 \\ - \partial_x A (g_1 - g_2) \big((\partial_t u)^2 - (\partial_x u)^2\big) \Big] \,\mathrm{d}x. \end{multline} Recall that $A(x)$ is constant for all $x>\ell$ so there are no incoming waves at $x=\ell$. This means that $(\partial_t + \partial_x) u (\ell, \tau)=0$. We also take the requirement \begin{equation} g_1(0) = g_2(0) = 1. \end{equation} Then the {boundary terms} satisfy \begin{align*} &\intlim{0}{\ell} \Big[ g_1 A (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2 - g_2 A (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2 \Big] \\ &= g_1(\ell) A(\ell) (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2(\ell,\tau) - g_2(\ell) A(\ell) (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2(\ell,\tau) \\ &\quad - g_1(0) A(0) (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2(0,\tau) + g_2(0) A(0) (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2(0,\tau) \\ &= 0 - g_2(\ell) A(\ell) (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2(\ell,\tau)- 4 \partial_t u(0,\tau) \partial_x u(0,\tau) \\ &= - g_2(\ell) A(\ell) (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2(\ell,\tau) - 4 \partial_t \Lambda_{\text{ND}} ( \phi) |_{t= \tau} \phi (\tau) . \end{align*} The first term on the right is always non-positive. Moreover, $\phi (\tau) = 0$ for $\tau > \max \operatorname{supp} \phi $ which implies that the second term vanishes for a such $\tau$. Thus, the {expression for boundary terms} above is, { in total,} non-positive for $\tau > \max \operatorname{supp} \phi $. We can also estimate the integrand of the remaining integral in (\ref{eq:energy-derivative-Calculation}) as follows \[ - \partial_x A (g_1 - g_2) \big((\partial_t u)^2 - (\partial_x u)^2\big) \leq \tfrac{1}{2} \abs{\partial_x A} \abs{g_1 - g_2} \big((\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2 + (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2\big). \] These then imply \begin{align*} &\mathscr{E}_{\phi, g_1,g_2}'(\tau) \leq \frac{1}{2} \int_0^\ell \parentheses*{-\partial_x g_1 + \frac{1}{2} \abs*{\frac{\partial_x A}{A}} \abs{g_1 - g_2}} (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2 A \,\mathrm{d}x \\ &\quad \frac{1}{2} \int_0^\ell \parentheses*{\partial_x g_2 + \frac{1}{2} \abs*{\frac{\partial_x A}{A}} \abs{g_1 - g_2}} (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2 A \,\mathrm{d}x. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate the energy, use the wave equation and integrate by parts; outgoing condition at $\ell$ and vanishing data sign the boundary terms.

nodes.name: Differentiate the energy
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate under the integral sign
nodes.statement: Because everything is smooth and bounded, we can differentiate under the integral sign. We get \begin{align*} &\mathscr{E}_{\phi,g_1,g_2}'(\tau) = \int_0^\ell \left[ g_1 (\partial_t u + \partial_x u) (\partial_t^2 u + \partial_t\partial_x u) + g_2 (\partial_t u - \partial_x u) (\partial_t^2 u - \partial_t\partial_x u) \right] A \,\mathrm{d}x \\ \end{align*}

nodes.name: Use the wave equation
nodes.statement_short: Substitute $\square_A u=0$ and integrate by parts to obtain (A.5)
nodes.statement: Applying $\square_A u = 0$ yields \begin{align*} \mathscr{E}_{\phi,g_1,g_2}'(\tau) &= \int_0^\ell \Big[ g_1 (\partial_t u + \partial_x u) \Big(\partial_x^2 u + \frac{\partial_x A}{A} \partial_x u \\ &\qquad\quad + \partial_t\partial_x u\Big) + g_2 (\partial_t u - \partial_x u) \Big(\partial_x^2 u + \frac{\partial_x A}{A} \partial_x u - \partial_t\partial_x u \Big) \Big] A \,\mathrm{d}x. \\ &= \int_0^\ell \Big[ g_1 (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)(\partial_x^2 u + \partial_x \partial_t u) + g_1 (\partial_t u + \partial_x u) \frac{\partial_x A}{A} \partial_x u \\ &\qquad\quad + g_2 (\partial_t u - \partial_x u) (\partial_x^2 u - \partial_x \partial_t u) + g_2 (\partial_t u - \partial_x u) \frac{\partial_x A}{A} \partial_x u \Big] A \,\mathrm{d}x \\ &= \frac{1}{2} \int_0^\ell \Big[ g_1 \partial_x (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2 - g_2 \partial_x (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2 + \frac{\partial_x A}{A} \big(g_1 (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2 - g_2 (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2\big) \\ &\qquad\qquad - \frac{\partial_x A}{A} (g_1 - g_2) \big((\partial_t u)^2 - (\partial_x u)^2 \big) \Big] A \,\mathrm{d}x \\ &= \frac{1}{2} \int_0^\ell \Big[ g_1 \partial_x \big( A (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2 \big) - g_2 \partial_x \big( A (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2 \big) - \partial_x A (g_1 - g_2) \big( (\partial_t u)^2 - (\partial_x u)^2 \big) \Big] \,\mathrm{d}x. \\ \end{align*} Further, integrating by parts leads to \begin{multline} \mathscr{E}_{\phi,g_1,g_2}'(\tau) = \frac{1}{2} \intlim{0}{\ell} \Big[ g_1 A (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2 - g_2 A (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2 \Big] \\ + \frac{1}{2} \int_0^\ell \Big[ -\partial_x g_1 A (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2 + \partial_x g_2 A (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2 \\ - \partial_x A (g_1 - g_2) \big((\partial_t u)^2 - (\partial_x u)^2\big) \Big] \,\mathrm{d}x. \end{multline}

nodes.name: Energy derivative (A.5)
nodes.statement: \mathscr{E}_{\phi,g_1,g_2}'(\tau) = \frac{1}{2} \intlim{0}{\ell} \Big[ g_1 A (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2 - g_2 A (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2 \Big] \\ + \frac{1}{2} \int_0^\ell \Big[ -\partial_x g_1 A (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2 + \partial_x g_2 A (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2 \\ - \partial_x A (g_1 - g_2) \big((\partial_t u)^2 - (\partial_x u)^2\big) \Big] \,\mathrm{d}x.
nodes.label: eq:energy-derivative-Calculation

nodes.name: Boundary terms non-positive
nodes.statement_short: Outgoing condition at $\ell$ and the normalisation (A.6) make the boundary terms non-positive
nodes.statement: Recall that $A(x)$ is constant for all $x>\ell$ so there are no incoming waves at $x=\ell$. This means that $(\partial_t + \partial_x) u (\ell, \tau)=0$. We also take the requirement \begin{equation} g_1(0) = g_2(0) = 1. \end{equation} Then the {boundary terms} satisfy \begin{align*} &\intlim{0}{\ell} \Big[ g_1 A (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2 - g_2 A (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2 \Big] \\ &= g_1(\ell) A(\ell) (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2(\ell,\tau) - g_2(\ell) A(\ell) (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2(\ell,\tau) \\ &\quad - g_1(0) A(0) (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2(0,\tau) + g_2(0) A(0) (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2(0,\tau) \\ &= 0 - g_2(\ell) A(\ell) (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2(\ell,\tau)- 4 \partial_t u(0,\tau) \partial_x u(0,\tau) \\ &= - g_2(\ell) A(\ell) (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2(\ell,\tau) - 4 \partial_t \Lambda_{\text{ND}} ( \phi) |_{t= \tau} \phi (\tau) . \end{align*} The first term on the right is always non-positive. Moreover, $\phi (\tau) = 0$ for $\tau > \max \operatorname{supp} \phi $ which implies that the second term vanishes for a such $\tau$. Thus, the {expression for boundary terms} above is, { in total,} non-positive for $\tau > \max \operatorname{supp} \phi $.

nodes.name: Estimate interior term
nodes.statement_short: Bound the remaining integrand
nodes.statement: We can also estimate the integrand of the remaining integral in (\ref{eq:energy-derivative-Calculation}) as follows \[ - \partial_x A (g_1 - g_2) \big((\partial_t u)^2 - (\partial_x u)^2\big) \leq \tfrac{1}{2} \abs{\partial_x A} \abs{g_1 - g_2} \big((\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2 + (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2\big). \] These then imply \begin{align*} &\mathscr{E}_{\phi, g_1,g_2}'(\tau) \leq \frac{1}{2} \int_0^\ell \parentheses*{-\partial_x g_1 + \frac{1}{2} \abs*{\frac{\partial_x A}{A}} \abs{g_1 - g_2}} (\partial_t u + \partial_x u)^2 A \,\mathrm{d}x \\ &\quad \frac{1}{2} \int_0^\ell \parentheses*{\partial_x g_2 + \frac{1}{2} \abs*{\frac{\partial_x A}{A}} \abs{g_1 - g_2}} (\partial_t u - \partial_x u)^2 A \,\mathrm{d}x. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Energy dissipation inequality
nodes.statement: If $g_1$ and $g_2$ additionally satisfy \begin{equation} \begin{cases} \phantom{-} \partial_x g_1 - \tfrac{M}{2} \abs{g_1 - g_2} \geq \lambda g_1 \\ - \partial_x g_2 - \tfrac{M}{2} \abs{g_1 - g_2} \geq \lambda g_2 , \end{cases} \end{equation} for $M = \max \abs{\partial_x A / A}$, we arrive at \begin{equation} \mathscr{E}_{\phi ,g_1, g_2}'(\tau) \leq - \lambda \mathscr{E}_{\phi,g_1,g_2}(\tau), \end{equation} whenever $\tau > \max \operatorname{supp} \phi$.

nodes.name: Weight inequalities (A.7)
nodes.statement: \begin{cases} \phantom{-} \partial_x g_1 - \tfrac{M}{2} \abs{g_1 - g_2} \geq \lambda g_1 \\ - \partial_x g_2 - \tfrac{M}{2} \abs{g_1 - g_2} \geq \lambda g_2 , \end{cases}
nodes.label: eq:energy-coefficient-inequalities

nodes.name: Energy dissipation (A.8)
nodes.statement: \mathscr{E}_{\phi ,g_1, g_2}'(\tau) \leq - \lambda \mathscr{E}_{\phi,g_1,g_2}(\tau),
nodes.label: eq:energy-derivative-estimate

nodes.name: Energy weights and exponential energy decay
nodes.statement: Let $M = \max \abs{A^{-1} \partial_x A}$ and $\lambda = \tfrac{M}{2} e^{-M \ell} \sqrt{1 - 2 M \ell e^{-2 M \ell}}$ where $\ell$ is the length of the domain of interest defined along with $\mathscr{E}_{\phi,g_1,g_2}$ in (\ref{eq:energy-def}). Set \begin{align} g_1(x) = \frac{e^{\frac{M}{2} x}}{\sqrt{\lambda^2 + \parentheses*{M/2}^2}} \Bigg(& \sqrt{\lambda^2 + \parentheses*{M/2}^2} \cosh \parentheses*{\sqrt{\lambda^2 + \parentheses*{M/2}^2} x} \\ & + \parentheses*{\lambda - M/2} \sinh \parentheses*{\sqrt{\lambda^2 + \parentheses*{M/2}^2} x} \Bigg) \end{align} \begin{align} g_2(x) = \frac{e^{\frac{M}{2} x}}{\sqrt{\lambda^2 + \parentheses*{M/2}^2}} \Bigg(& \sqrt{\lambda^2 + \parentheses*{M/2}^2} \cosh \parentheses*{\sqrt{\lambda^2 + \parentheses*{M/2}^2} x} \\ & - \parentheses*{\lambda + M/2} \sinh \parentheses*{\sqrt{\lambda^2 + \parentheses*{M/2}^2} x} \Bigg) \end{align} Then $g_1$ and $g_2$ are strictly positive on $[0,\ell]$, and they satisfy (\ref{eq:energy-coefficient-zero-values}) and (\ref{eq:energy-coefficient-inequalities}). As a consequence, (\ref{eq:energy-derivative-estimate}) holds for $\tau > \tau_0:= \max \operatorname{supp} \phi $ and hence \begin{equation} \mathscr{E}_{\phi,g_1,g_2}(\tau) \leq \mathscr{E}_{\phi,g_1,g_2}(\tau_0) e^{-\lambda (\tau-\tau_0)} \end{equation} by Gr\"onwall's inequality.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit positive weights $g_1,g_2$ satisfy the dissipation inequalities, so by Gronwall the energy decays like $e^{-\lambda(\tau-\tau_0)}$.
nodes.label: gronw-lemma

nodes.name: Weight g_1 (A.9)
nodes.statement: g_1(x) = \frac{e^{\frac{M}{2} x}}{\sqrt{\lambda^2 + \parentheses*{M/2}^2}} \Bigg(& \sqrt{\lambda^2 + \parentheses*{M/2}^2} \cosh \parentheses*{\sqrt{\lambda^2 + \parentheses*{M/2}^2} x} \\ & + \parentheses*{\lambda - M/2} \sinh \parentheses*{\sqrt{\lambda^2 + \parentheses*{M/2}^2} x} \Bigg)

nodes.name: Weight g_2 (A.11)
nodes.statement: g_2(x) = \frac{e^{\frac{M}{2} x}}{\sqrt{\lambda^2 + \parentheses*{M/2}^2}} \Bigg(& \sqrt{\lambda^2 + \parentheses*{M/2}^2} \cosh \parentheses*{\sqrt{\lambda^2 + \parentheses*{M/2}^2} x} \\ & - \parentheses*{\lambda + M/2} \sinh \parentheses*{\sqrt{\lambda^2 + \parentheses*{M/2}^2} x} \Bigg)

nodes.name: Exponential energy decay (A.13)
nodes.statement: \mathscr{E}_{\phi,g_1,g_2}(\tau) \leq \mathscr{E}_{\phi,g_1,g_2}(\tau_0) e^{-\lambda (\tau-\tau_0)}

nodes.statement: Let $a>0$. Integrating again in $x$ yields \begin{align} \int_0^a A(x) p (x,t_0 + a) dx = - \int_{t_0}^{t_0 + a} u(a,t) dt + \int_{t_0}^{t_0 + a} u(0,t) dt . \end{align} Since the wave $w$ satisfies $w|_{t = t_0} = 0 = \partial_t w|_{t = t_0}$, it vanishes in the wedge $\{ (x,t) \in (0,\infty) \times \mathbb{R} : t -t_0 < x \}$. Consequently, the first term on the right in \eqref{ad00} vanishes and we deduce \begin{align} \int_0^a A(x) p (x,t_0 + a) dx = \int_{t_0}^{t_0 + a} u(0,t) dt . \end{align} This is the equation (3) in \cite{sondhi_gopinath}. As $A(0) = 1$, it coincides with \begin{align} \int_0^a A(x) p (x,t_0 + a) dx = \int_{t_0}^{t_0 + a} f(t) dt , . \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Integrating the system twice and using finite speed of propagation gives $\int_0^a A p(x,t_0+a)dx=\int_{t_0}^{t_0+a} f\,dt$ (Sondhi-Gopinath eq. (3)).
